utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The witness is not in? Is there something to be raised? Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning. I wanted to clarify something about the exhibits from the last -- or, pardon. [Interpretation] I would like to clarify certain issues relating to the comments about the previous witness. However, Mr. Robinson explained to me that everything was all right. However, as far as this witness is concerned, I kindly ask you to reconsider the issue of the time allocated to him. His statement has a huge number of paragraphs where he has given arbitrary assessment. Here, we have him as an expert with authority. Okay, he is a witness in this case, but he was an expert in another case. So all these statements have to be clarified by the Defence, and the witness is going to be asked to provide additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us bring in the witness. All I can say at this moment, we'll stick to the time-limit which has been allowed for the moment, and we'll see how you will be going with the witness. Unless there's extraordinary circumstances warranting a further extension, we'll stick to the time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're bringing in the witness, if I could just indicate that yesterday we received a motion for videolink testimony of Thorbjorn Overgard. And I've discussed that with Dr. Karadzic, and we don't object to that. We could just let you know that right now. And we are also hoping that we can arrange a videolink interview of the witness before he testifies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Konings. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Would you be able to give us your full name for the trial record, please?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: My name is Harry Konings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Konings, is it correct that you've been serving with the Royal Netherlands Army for the last 40 years and presently hold the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from May until October 1995, did you work as a United Nations Military Observer, or UNMO, as part of the UN mission in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about the evidence you've previously given to the ICTY relating to your experiences and observations in Sarajevo. First, do you recall giving statements to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal in 1996 and again in 2006?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do recall the fact that I gave statements then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you testify before Trial Chambers of this Tribunal in the case of Dragomir Milosevic in 2007 and during the trial of Momcilo Perisic in 2009, all relating to your service as an UNMO in Sarajevo in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did testify in those two cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on November 11th of this year, did you sign a further statement for the Office of the Prosecutor consolidating elements of this previously-recorded evidence as it related to Sarajevo, with some additional information and references to a number of documents?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I have signed that further statement on the 11th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you review that statement again in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have reviewed that statement in preparation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On reviewing it, did you have any corrections, or modifications, or other changes to make to that document?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no further corrections or modifications to make to this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if you were asked the same questions today which gave rise to that written evidence, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I will try to do the utmost to give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That being the case, then, Your Honours, could I ask that the 11 November amalgamated statement of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, 65 ter 90202, be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1953, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of the written evidence of the witness. From April until October 1995, Lieutenant-Colonel Harry Konings served as a United Nations Military Observer in Sarajevo. He was posted to the Sarajevo Central or SC-1 team, where he held the position of team leader for most of his tour. During that tour, the witness investigated at least 100 shelling and sniping incidents, of which he estimates 40 or 50 involved civilian casualties. The greater part his investigations concerned shelling. The witness explains that the members of SC-1 attended incident sites together with local Sarajevo police forces; however, they conducted separate investigations. In addition to the examination of the scene, the UNMOs from SC-1 would also examine the wounded and corpses in hospitals and morgues. They would prepare reports on their investigations, which were forwarded to the UNMO chain of command. Those reports were analysed at headquarters level, where conclusions were then arrived at as to origins of fire. In many cases, they were able to make the conclusion that the fire came from Serb territory, while in some cases, they were not able to make any conclusions as to the source of fire. Sometimes the UNMOs, based on information available, could form their own conclusions. The witness never personally saw any fire outgoing from Bosnian-held territory, nor did he investigate scenes where it was confirmed that the ABiH was the source of fire. According to the witness, civilian life in Sarajevo was extremely difficult due to random fire by Bosnian Serb forces into civilian areas. The witness investigated at least two modified air-bomb incidents and recalls the highly inaccurate and destructive nature of these weapons. In these cases, his observations at the scene led him to conclude that these air-bombs were fired from Bosnian Serb positions. The witness and his team from SC-1 participated in the investigation of the second Markale Market incident on 28 August 1995. He recalls seeing the very clear crater at the point of impact, immediately recognisable as a crater from a mortar projectile, and the tail of the projectile nearby. From the crater analysis, the witness could determine the direction of fire, but not the origin. However, coupled with the fact that SC-1's observation post in the same direction had detected no outgoing shots from Bosnian-held territory that day, the witness is of the view that the origin of fire of the killing-round and other rounds fired that morning came from within Bosnian Serb-held territory. That's the summary of evidence. And now, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, if I may, I'd like to ask you a number of questions in relation to some aspects of your 11 November statement. If we could first have 65 ter 14809 on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you see an image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise that image?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I recognise that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- and the image being a map, could you tell us what the map depicts?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The map depicts a larger part of the city of Sarajevo, especially the central part, and it reflects the major part of the area of operations of Sierra Charlie 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I see in red there's a triangle marked on the middle of the page with the letters in red "OP-1." Do you know how that marking came to be on this map?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In the Dragomir Milosevic case, I marked that spot on the map being the location of Observation Post number 1, the observation post that was occupied by Sierra Charlie 1 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever serve at that observation post?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on quite a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you describe the area around the observation post, the surroundings, for us?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The observation post was located at the -- in the hills quite high above the city of Sarajevo. The view from the observation post was directed to the north and the north-east and the north-west, and we had a very good view on the larger part of the city of Sarajevo, even to the west and to the east, but especially to the central part and the confrontation line in the north of the city. The view was not blocked by any obstructions. The observation post was located in the outskirts -- in the wider outskirts of the city of Sarajevo. There were no, really, obstructions between the OP-1 and the view that we had on the larger part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember where OP-1 was in relation to confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The confrontation line at the south part of the city was running on top of the hills at the backside of OP-1, let's say about 500, 600 metres above the backside -- the south side of OP-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1954, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now have 65 ter 10258.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to refresh your memory, Lieutenant-Colonel, in your written evidence at paragraph 12, you referred to a series of photographs that you took during your tour in Sarajevo, and I'd like to deal with three of those, this being the first one. Now, do you see the image on the photograph or a photograph on the screen in front of you, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you just talked about and described in detail the view from OP-1, and I wonder if you could tell us what this photograph represents.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This photograph is taken from OP-1. It's taken in a northern -- a general northern direction, and it shows the larger part of, let's say, Eastern Sarajevo, with the central part around the letter A, Alpha. That part has been marked as an example during the Milosevic case to highlight the old library, which is in the old part of the city and which was a fine mark for us to have an idea where we -- where everything in the city was. The part marked with B is the area where our team base was located, the team base from Sierra Charlie 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the general area of the city that your team base was situated in?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That area was called Sedrenik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move on to another photo, please, 65 ter 10412. And just on the transcript, line 17, "Sedrenik" should be spelled S-e-d-r-e-n-i-k. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a further photograph now, Lieutenant-Colonel, on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do see a picture, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, this picture has been taken by myself again from OP-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does it represent the same area that we saw in the photo immediately prior, P1955?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Actually, this -- this photograph can be connected to the former picture, to the former photograph, and it depicts a more western area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this please be the next Prosecution exhibit .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go on to one final photograph, 65 ter 10259, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see the image on the screen in front of you, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do see the image.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the photo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah. That picture has been taken by one of my colleagues and depicts the actual place where we observed from OP-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you explain -- are you in a position to explain the red circle marked with the letter A on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The red circle marked with A are the twin towers in the very western part of the city, the newer part of the city very close to the Holiday Inn Hotel, which shows that we had a very wide view and a clear view to the larger part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This photographs shows three persons. Do you know who these three persons are?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The two persons at the right, without any head cover, are two Danish soldiers which were helping us in building a kind of cover on OP-1, because there was no cover whatsoever. We were standing in the open, and we needed some cover, so the soldiers were helping us. And the third person with the head cover, that I'm -- that's myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we also tender this photograph, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Leaving now the photographs, Lieutenant-Colonel, I'd like to turn to your involvement in the investigation of the shelling incident that we'll refer to as Markale II on 28 August 1995. Do you remember, Lieutenant-Colonel, when you arrived at the scene in relation to the explosion, itself?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I arrived about 40 minutes after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you describe the scene when you got there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: When we came at the scene, all the bodies were removed, but there was still body parts at the scene of the explosion. There were a lot of people around. We were not the only UN soldiers. There were also French engineers doing their own investigation. We were there together with Bosnian police, and it was a quite very tense situation. The civilians that were on the scene, many of them were quite hostile towards us, towards everybody wearing a blue helmet or a blue beret. Well, it was a very tense and very difficult situation over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Talking about the scene, I'd like you to turn your head, please, and look at the photomontage sitting beside you to your right, which, for the record, bears the 65 ter number 09533. Lieutenant-Colonel, do you recognise this? Is this something you've previously seen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I've seen this photo composition before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was at various times in the preparation for this -- for the trial session of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise it? What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It depicts the overall scene of the place where the Markale incident -- the Markale II incident took place in the main street in Sarajevo. In the middle, the crater of the exploding mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To what extent does it resemble, to your recollection, the scene as you first saw it on 28 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, it resembles the scene quite clearly, with the exception that when I was there, there were, of course, a lot of people walking around on the street doing whatever they had to do over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that this photograph shows the crater. Could you indicate the crater to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I can. The crater is over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the witness has pointed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you up-load in the e-court as well while we are using that one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. The witness, for the record, has pointed to a location on the ground that appears to be marked -- outlined in white markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you make any observations about the crater at the time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We made the regular observations that we always did, doing crater analysis, which is, first of all, establish whether it was an artillery or mortar projectile. In this case, we came to the conclusion that it was originated -- it was made by a mortar projectile. Further things that we did, just as regular as we did it every time when we did a crater analysis, is building an opinion on the direction of fire and trying to find remnants, shrapnels, or part of the originated projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just for the moment, could we call up the image of 09533 in e-court, and the witness can actually then circle the crater that he had indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, are you -- you're familiar with the e-court technology. Could you please draw a circle around the mortar crater that you had indicated, marking that with a red circle?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 09533, then, as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of the zooming in, we lost some part of the left side. Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the Prosecution's purposes, I'm fine with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be exhibited as P1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Konings, if you could kindly put the date of today, which is 7th of December, 2010, and your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the picture, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, you indicated that you were able to come to the conclusion that the crater had been made by a mortar projectile. On what basis did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's a combination of training and a combination of experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what experience, in particular?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The fact that on the 28th of August, I was already in Sarajevo for a longer period, and I was not the only one on the spot. I was there with a patrol team of my -- of my UNMO team, and we all came together to the conclusion that this was a mortar projectile because the crater of a mortar, in comparison with artillery projectiles, is quite specific. And on this moment in time, I had seen already several mortar projectiles -- mortar craters before, so, well, it's a combination of training and expertise, experience, that you come to the conclusion that this is a mortar projectile crater.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you notice any irregular features to this crater or any signs of tampering during the course of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. We came to the conclusion that this was a very clear -- I would even use the word "ideal" mortar crater. It was very clear. It was -- there was no signs of tampering or whatever. So we came right away to the conclusion that it was a mortar crater, as did the French UNMO soldiers on the same spot, where we had a short conversation with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the calibre or size of the weapon that made the crater, did you and your team make any determinations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. My patrol of my team, we came to the conclusion that it was a 120-millimetre projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The most important point to find that was that we found the mortar tail, which is very specific to a 120 or to any other calibre, which we found quite close to the area of impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Similarly, in the course of the investigations did you and your patrol make any determinations as to the direction from which this mortar was fired?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. In the same way we did all our investigation, we used a compass to come to the conclusion that the direction was 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the map, roughly, what does a finding of 170 degrees represent?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, if you take 180 degrees as due south, 170 is almost due south.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you conduct any other shelling investigations that same day?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We did another investigation after this one, quite close to this location, where there was an impact of four additional 120-millimetre mortar projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we now, then, look at 65 ter 14812, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, now you see another map in front of you which bears the marking of OP-1 and a number of additional markings in red. Do you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's also a map which was used in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know how the markings came to be on that map?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I made the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention to the points numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, could you tell us what they represent, then?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Point number 5 reflects the Markale II rounds, the rounds that we were discussing before. 1, 2, 3, 4 -- the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 reflect the other four rounds that we investigated at a later time-frame on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that those other shells were quite close to -- fell quite close to the market-place. Are you in a position to -- or do you recall, approximately, the distance in metres of these shells, these four from the fifth one?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not exactly anymore, but it was less than 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you and your patrol make any findings as to the bearing or direction from which these four mortars were fired?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: These four mortars, we came to the conclusion that they came from a general direction 220 to 240 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as you did with the shell that fell on the Markale Market, could you perhaps indicate for us, roughly, what that might represent on the map, in terms of direction?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, if 180 degrees is due south, 220 to 240 is, let's say, roughly south-west.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel -- before I move on, actually, could I have this map, please, marked as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, did you, yourself, come to any conclusions as to the actual origin of fire of these five shells?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Not on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you reach any conclusion at a later time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. In combination with the findings of my observers on OP-1, we had two observers on that day over there, and later on the day and on the 29th we had a discussion with each other. We came to the conclusion that these rounds came from Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis, Lieutenant-Colonel, did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We concentrated, first of all, on round number 5 on the Markale II round, and if you take a bearing of 170 degrees, it brings the line of fire towards the area where OP-1 is, at least in the vicinity, less than one kilometre from that away. As it was a very clear day, a very quiet day on the 28th of August, there was no shelling, no firing, there was an excellent view. It was a bright day. The OP-1 observers would have noticed anything that would have happened in Bosnian Army territory on outgoing rounds. Firing a 120-millimetre mortar is something that you will notice, especially when it's in your vicinity, even the vicinity of one kilometre. The fact that those two observers didn't hear anything, didn't notice any outgoing rounds, no explosion, no smoke, no flash, we came to the conclusion that the round number 5 must have come from the other side of the mountains and the mountains muffled the sound of the outgoing round, the actual firing of a round. That was -- so in a combination of information, the fact that we found the bearing, 170, and the fact that those two observers didn't see or hear anything in their wider vicinity, we came to the conclusion that it was a round coming from Bosnian Serb-held territory behind the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just in relation to what you've just explained, I have two questions, the first being in relation to your statement of the fact that these two observers didn't hear anything. What kind of noise does the firing of a 120-millimetre mortar make, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to describe, but it's -- it's a loud noise, and I can assure you, I have a lot of experience with that. You will hear it if it's fired in the area around OP-1, especially on such an absolute silent, bright day with hardly any wind. So the sound is not muffled, the sound is not dragged away. In fact, I should take you to the artillery firing range here in the Netherlands and show you or let you hear whatever the sound is. You need cover for that, even when you are on a wider distance. It's a loud -- very loud bang. I cannot describe it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And talking about your observers who were in OP-1 that day, what were their names?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: They were two of my observers. One was a Norwegian, and that was Thomas [Realtime transcript read in error "Klustat"], and the other one was an Irish major. That was Paul Conway.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: And the name of the Norwegian is Knustadt, it's not "Klustat." It's wrongly spelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look now, please, at 65 ter 09911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, could you give us the spelling of that Norwegian officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I -- I spell it with the military alphabet, which is Kilo-November-Uniform-Sierra-Tango-Alpha-Delta-Tango.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Knustadt.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You see a document now, Lieutenant-Colonel, on the screen in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second spelling should be N --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's K-n-u-s-t-a-d-t. No, it's not an O; a U.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise the document that now appears on the screen in front of you, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It's a so-called UNMO patrol report, written on the 29th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I take you over to the next page, please. It's difficult to read, but I wonder if I could take you to point 2 under paragraph 4. If you could tell us what that represents.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This report was -- sorry. This report was written on 29th, after we had a meeting with the special Bosnian committee that investigated the Markale incident of the 28th. And point number 4 reflects the most important subjects that were discussed during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what does point 2(a) indicate?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, it's nearly impossible for me to read it, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the Bench can read it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a typewritten version?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if we can't find one immediately, Your Honour, we'll certainly provide one as soon as possible. I wonder if I could just ask for what I think might be a duplicate entry, a duplicate 65 ter number, and we could see if that can be displayed more clearly. 14356. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 65 ter number has no image in it, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Actually, be read -- should it be read in Serbian and then through the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid may be able to help us in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic. Your words were not translated, but I -- the problem is that the witness is not able to read Serbian. So can we deal with other things first, and then we come back to this later on. But if you can move on, I'll leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll move on. And, frankly, the document is explored within the amalgamated statement, so what I'll do is I'll move on to the final area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, in paragraph 65 of your written evidence, there you set out the times of the impact of each of those shells that you had indicated on the previous exhibit. And the paragraph, just for ease of reference, I'll read it to you. The paragraph reads as follows: "In my Perisic testimony, I marked the location of each of the impacts, 65 ter 14812, according to the grid references listed on page 3 of Exhibit P150 in this case. The first shell landed at 1050 hours, with the coordinates BP927590, and is marked 1; the second at 1050 hours, BP927591, marked 2; third, at 1100 hours, BP928591, marked 3; fourth at 1100 hours, BP928591, marked 4; and fifth, the shot that hit Markale at 1114 hours, BP927594, marked 5." Now, hearing that again, do you remember that evidence, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, my question -- I've read this to focus you on the timing that you indicated in your written evidence, and I wonder whether you see any indication between the timing of these first four shells and the timing of the shell that hit the market-place.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, the first four rounds seemed to have a certain combination towards each other, because they all fell roughly in the same area and with some time separation in between, so they could be estimated, but I don't have, of course, the exact proof of that. But you can estimate them to be an adjust fire - that's one possibility - which could be -- which one could have used in order to fire, with the correct data, the fifth round on a different spot, which is not an unusual military method is to adjust fire on one location and to do the end fire, the fire for effect, at another location. That's a matter of military procedure, that you don't want an enemy to see that you are adjusting fire on one spot, knowing that the fire for effect will come on the same spot. So it's a matter of -- I don't have the problem English word for that, but it's a matter of disguise somebody in order to make him not aware what you are -- what your intentions are. That's a possibility. I do not have the proof for that, but that's an estimation you can make. One other estimation is that the four rounds are aimed against a separate target, one of the buildings that was in that area. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before concluding, Mr. Reid has invited us to try 65 ter 09911. Again, the version that's up-loaded may be slightly better, and we'll have a look shortly to see. Could we just move over to the second page, please. I think the more prudent course of action would be to have this re-scanned, Your Honour. I don't find it to be particularly legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we zoom in further on the English version, I think that that can be read, possibly. Why don't we collapse, for the moment, the Serbian version at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, not bad. Could you just - thank you - scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Humanitarian points. Now we can read it. Could you read for us, Lieutenant-Colonel, what you wrote on item number 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You want me to read the complete item, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Number 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to do my best. "Participants of the meeting, see annex to this report, including Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. The aim of the meeting was to compare the reports made by UNMO patrol and the rest of the investigation team (between representatives of various Bosnian authorities)." Point number 2 reads: "Following aspects were not mentioned in the first report and can be mentioned as UNMO confirmed." Under point A: "In the time-frame of the five impacts, UNMOs of India Charlie Zulu team working on OP-1 saw or heard no outgoing mortar rounds, neither from Bosnian Army territory (general area," that I cannot read, and the second thing is "Colina Kapa), nor from Bosnian Serb Army territory." "The minimum" -- under point B: "The minimum angle of impact of the 120-millimetre mortar projectile which hit near the market-place, grid 927594, was 67 degrees." Three: "The patrol leader received a list of killed and injured people (35 killed and 78 wounded)." This -- I think that this says "topics," no, I cannot read that. "... are added as an annex. See also patrol leader's remarks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just on this, then -- and thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Two questions. What's the India Charlie Zulu team?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's the new name for the Sierra Charlie 1 team. Somewhere in August, we had to change names.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that this was your second report. Why was this information not included in the first report?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Because the first report was written directly after our first investigation on the 28th of August, and the information in this report was an additional information, because only in the evening or in the morning of the 29th I had the opportunity to talk in person with my observers from OP-1. Before that, I only talked with them by radio, and we kept radio exchange information very short because we knew that all parties involved in the conflict were listening on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does this report of yours, then, reflect the totality of the information that led you to your conclusions as to the origin of fire of the killing-round?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, this report has to be seen in direct conjunction with the first report made on the 28th. They are connected towards each other. For that reason, I refer to that as well. And those two reports together, after having discussed the whole matter with my UNMOs from OP-1, we came to the conclusion for ourselves that the rounds came from Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1960, Exhibit P1960.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, then, Your Honours. If we could perhaps deal with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Amongst them, some of the items have been already admitted. That will be 99117, 10294, and, finally, 40221.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one final item I'd like to raise is 14345, which is a record of investigation of the Stari Grad, 29th of August, 1995. I take it this is a report about an unscheduled incident, and it has been our practice not to admit those reports. Is there any specific reason for this item to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour. The document, Your Honour, records the fact that Lieutenant-Colonel Konings took part in this investigation, alongside local officials. The lieutenant-colonel has already given evidence to that effect in his written statement. So for that reason, I don't see any need for 65 ter 14345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, he refers to this incident in paragraph 70, so I think that's sufficient. So we admitted six of them already, so the remaining items will be about six, so that will be -- unless there's any objections, that will be admitted and given a number by the Court Deputy in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, now it's for you to cross-examine the lieutenant-colonel, but don't take it for granted that your time will be extended. So you should try your best not to omit important things on your part to be cross-examined. Let us begin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Lieutenant-Colonel. I believe I'll be speaking for many in the courtroom if I ask that this current temperature setting will -- should be saved for August, but currently we need something warmer. I feel a chill and a wind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I've been advised it will be warmed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I would like to thank you for meeting with the Defence and sharing with us precious information about doctrine and about details. To save time, I will structure my questions in such a way that you are able to answer yes or no, especially in the part covered by our interview. Could you refute or confirm some of the following points that I noted down during our meeting. I will read in English. You said: [In English] "It would be legitimate to harass forces of the enemy if it was directed toward military targets." You said that: "It was legitimate to use artillery and mortars to frighten the enemy." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I assume that you were referring to the meeting we had last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, September last year.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not able to answer you in plain yes or no. You might require that from me, but I do not have that possibility. And I would like to stress to Your Honours that that meeting took place more than one year ago, and as far as I'm concerned, that was a very informal meeting, which I accepted to do so with the permission of my Ministry of Defence. And I, personally, have made no further notes of that meeting, and for that reason it is very hard for me to recall everything from what has been said there, especially since the purpose of that meeting was, on the request of Mr. Karadzic, to have an informal meeting and to ask me certain questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Konings. Mr. Karadzic, I'm wondering where you are leading, whether it's legitimate to harass the force of enemy if it was directed toward military target. The witness hasn't come as a legal expert. This is not the witness to explore such questions. You cannot complain on the shortage of time, asking these questions. Come to your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect, I only wanted to say that what applied then, as far as what was legitimate in Sarajevo, applies today still. So it doesn't matter whether the interview was last year or more recently. I just wanted this witness to present to the Trial Chamber what constitutes legitimate action on a battle-field. And there are several important matters in that area, but I will move to something else if you wish, and then I'll see if we can come back to it and clear up these points or perhaps clear them up as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the front-line ran through the urban area through the town and sometimes even bisected a building, and that it was sometimes impossible to tell which party was firing?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm any specifics on the front-line running through buildings because that was not in my part of Sarajevo. I know that in certain areas, there were reports that the front-line ran through buildings, but I was not stationed in that area. I was stationed in the old part of the city, where we had no such situation. In my area of operations, as we call an area of a team - that's a military term - the confrontation line was running, let's say, outside the outskirts of the city. So in my area, we had not such a situation, and so I cannot judge whether that happened, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But speaking of your part of the city, is it true that the confrontation line followed one another and meandered through the city, around the hills and over the hills?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Generically speaking, the confrontation line in my area was running on the hills around the north, the east, and the western -- and the southern part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did there exist a single section of the line that was not covered by another line? Was there a single section of a Muslim defence line, for instance, that was not crossed by a Serbian line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do not think I understand the question, what you mean by using the word "that was not crossed by a Serbian line."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's up to the interpreters, or perhaps I was not precise enough. Is it fair to say that wherever there was one line, it faced the opposite party's line, so the one line is not "crossed" but "overlapped by" or "facing" another line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In my generic recollection, but that's very limited, the confrontation lines of both armies were facing each other all along my area of operations. But I have to add to that that our main effort of my UNMO team was towards the city, itself. We were not allowed to do anything in the vicinity of the confrontation line, for various reasons. We were not allowed to do so by our own UN organisation, due to the danger that was involved in that, and we were not allowed to come close to the confrontation line, due to the restriction of movement imposed upon us by the Bosnian Army. So my knowledge of the confrontation line and the exact running of the confrontation line is limited, is very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that you told us that you were not aware of any disproportionate fire from the Serbian forces during your tenure there?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do not recall that I said that. I don't think I used the word "disproportionate fire from the Serbian forces" in any occasion. I don't think I understand your question quite well, so I really appreciate that I can re-evaluate what you ask. In fact, I think I said that the Serbs used disproportionate fire, if I understand the word "disproportionate" correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Lieutenant-Colonel, you told us that you had not observed any disproportionate fire from the Serbian side. But tell me this: Is it true that you said that there was no official characterisation by the UN that Sarajevo was a city under siege?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I never said that. I never used the word -- the statement that the UN in any way characterised officially that UN [sic] was a city under siege. If I have used the word "siege," that was on my own -- on my own knowledge. I have nothing to add to that further. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what you told us during the interview. Is it true that you spent most of your time at Sedrenik and that you were barely aware of events in the rest of the city?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Again, if you refer to the interview that we had last year, I have a real problem with referring to that constantly, because as I said before, for me that's an informal discussion that we had between two of us and I made no note whatsoever on that speech. So I really would appreciate if we can refer to official documents that have been used before, and if you have anything that I have -- should have said to you, I would like to read that once more, I would like to appreciate that. So it is hardly impossible to recall a conversation that we had more than one year ago, which I did on my own appreciation, but I really would like to refer to the whole situation that I'm here for today, to official documents, as the Office of the Prosecution has done before. So if you recall something or if you refer to something, I would like to have it in reading and not only from your recollection or from your own notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. Konings. Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, it's time for you to ask specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it be easier for you if we gave you a summary of that interview, because this is not about what you told us then, but what you meant then and what you mean now, what you knew then and what you know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then that interview was of absolutely no use at all, it was pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you said on one occasion that it was your task to observe and report everything going on in the city; is that right? Let me remind you. You said that in your evidence on the 12th of March, 2007, in the Milosevic trial, page 3549. "... and the most important task was to be the impartial eye-witness of UNPROFOR inside the city of Sarajevo and give reports on every incident or every happening that occurred in the city."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's possible that you show me that evidence on the screen, Your Honour. I just would like to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I offer this hard copy to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it part of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's part of his testimony on 12 March 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we have it in the e-court?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because we were taken aback to hear that the witness does not recall the things he had said about the doctrine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It cannot be an excuse. But on this occasion, for the sake of time, why don't we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 22281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we raise the page a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Starting with line 25, look at the passage that is underlined and bold. Did you say this in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, to make clear why I insist on having this in front of me: I have done many statements before in 2007 and 2009. I want to make absolutely sure that I understand the questions that are asked of me so that I can give the proper and correct answer. And reading this, I've said that, and I still agree with that, that this was our main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I then be right in saying that you were supposed to observe and report the events between SC-1 and OP-1, that is, in the old town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We had a specific area of operations that was outlined to us and that was generically spoken, the area between Sierra Charlie 1 and OP-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to Markale, we need to shed light on a couple of other matters primarily linked to methodology. On page 2 of your statement from 1996, you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We can remove that document from the ELMO. But just for the record, can we know the page number of that page? Can we see the page number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The top part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We should see the top part, yes. 3549.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just note that the line numbering appears to be a little off on this -- that page displayed, and I was just trying to figure out the reasons why with Mr. Reid. And I have that text on pages 3552 and 3553 of the 65 ter number I just gave Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the old days, the e-court numbers were not consistent with the hard-copy numbers. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I also processed the text further to put it in bold, so it may have changed the numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you then state, in 1996: "I estimate that I investigated at least --" [In English] " ... in between 75 and 100 incidents, both shelling and sniping."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your reading was not fully translated. Could you read it again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the lieutenant-colonel be given a hard copy, and I will quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the statement from 1996, you said you estimated that you conducted investigations into 75 to 100 incidents of both shelling and sniping; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I just want to check. Yes, I see that in the -- on page 2 of that document of 1996. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you kindly look at page 2 of your 1996 statement, where you say that you conducted investigations into 150 to 200 shelling incidents.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't see that on page 2 of the 1996 document, but I might be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm looking in the wrong document. Can you point me out which point that is, which point you mean on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, at the top, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. If that's in the statement, I've said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, I'm concerned by a certain ease with which things are discussed, things that should be very legally precise. We should narrow down our discussion to things that you directly saw or heard. Do you agree? Do you agree that this is a significant discrepancy? You said that you investigated between 150 and 200 shelling incidents only - that's in the 2006 statement - and in the other statement you say the total incidents investigated was between 75 and 100?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I redirected that also in my later statement in November 2010, and I brought the number down, I think, to about 100 investigations that I did on shelling incidents. But I cannot recall them all, and I don't -- in various statements that I made, and especially the last one in 2010, because I gave it a good -- a good thought, a good thought over what happened, it is -- it is somewhere around 100, 120. I really don't recall that, but it is a substantial number where I'm talking about. I have been investigated by the Tribunal in a variety of occasions between 1996, where I stated that I did about 100 shelling incidents, and between -- recently in 2010, so you must -- you should understand that this is a difficulty to recall it all. And as I redirected my statement in the 2010 statement about -- I thought I said there were about 100, but the OTP can help me with that, I think that's the fair number that I should use. And I do not recall why I used the number of 150 to -- around 150 in 2006. I really do not have a recollection about that. But that I witnessed and that I investigated a fairly large number of crater -- of incidents in the city of Sarajevo, I think that might be very clear, and that exceeds at least the number that I recalled in 1996, which is the closest to my remember [sic] after 1995, and the corrected one that I used in 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you wrote in your 2010 statements is like this: "Although I haven't kept a detailed record, I've easily conducted more than 100 shelling investigations of mortar and artillery impacts, and three or four air-bomb impact investigations in Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the best I can recollect, Your Honour, in what happened. The times over there in 1995 were very tense, were very busy, so that it's impossible to have a recount of the exact number that I did. And I didn't keep note of everything I did during those days, but I think it's fair to say -- it's just to say not fair. It's very just to say that I did that number of at least 100 investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that it was tense and that you were very busy, you frequently mention, especially in relation to Markale, that you conducted your investigation in very hard -- very difficult conditions and under pressure, pressure from the personages around you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know what -- what the question is, Your Honour. There was a lot of pressure, but -- which is normal in a war situation, that there is a lot of pressure from various sides, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I paraphrased what you said; namely, that you carried out investigations, especially the one in Markale, briefly and under pressure of the surrounding people.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I phrased it in that way, so I would like to read that. But the pressure was coming from various sides. There was, of course, time pressure. Because it was a very serious incident, there was the pressure of the fact that - and that was always the fact - when you were on the scene of an explosion, more projectiles could follow. So that was the pressure that you had as well, to be as quick as possible, which makes a time constraint, which brings you a time pressure. You had to work very quickly because you were in danger on a certain spot. Where one round falls, more rounds can falls. And on this occasion, seeing the seriousness of the -- of what happened over there, it brought a lot of pressure, yes. It was tense, people were angry. My own superiors were there, and they were putting pressure on me to work exactly and to work fast to come up with my investigation results as soon as possible. And so there were -- there was pressure from many sides. And, yes, I do not deny there was pressure also from the Bosnian authorities who were present there, the judge from the Superior Court, in order to work quickly, yes, but that was caused by the whole tense situation over there and the seriousness of the thing that happened over there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is it time for a break or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll break for half an hour, resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'd like to ask the Chamber's permission at the next break to have Colonel Konings review a report of the interview that Dr. Karadzic had with him in September of 2009. I've actually prepared hard copies to be distributed to the Chamber. And this -- I took notes during that meeting and then prepared a contemporaneous report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When did you produce this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In September of 2009, two days after the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it disclosed to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been disclosed. It was disclosed to them just now. And it's -- normally we don't prepare these for anything other than memorialising what was said, but since there seems to be some discrepancies between what Colonel Konings recalls having been said and what we recall having been said, we'd like to have the opportunity to have him review that and then have Dr. Karadzic be able to put to him some of those things that could either be understood as agreed by him or perhaps be inconsistent statements with what he's testifying to now. So in order to lay the foundation for that, we would like the opportunity for him to review the statement at the next break and then be questioned about it after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember, Mr. Tieger, you rose at one point in time. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I rose initially, Your Honour, because I didn't consider it appropriate to be distributing that to the Chamber even before the request had been considered. Secondly, this is -- to the extent that the Defence wanted the witness to consider what he was purported to have said and clarify it, that could have and should have been done previously, not under the time pressure that exists today and after he's taken the stand. And the Prosecution considers this an inappropriate, belated effort to create an impeachment document that cannot serve as such under these circumstances, and an appropriate procedure would have been, clearly, to clarify it with the witness at the time of the interview, determine whether or not he agreed with the propositions presented in this document or any other document that the Defence considered memorialised some aspects of the statement, and give him a fair opportunity to consider that and clarify it at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I -- before the decision, may I say just one word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't like to waste our time. If you don't mind, if you could read this document during the break, and the accused may put any questions in relation to that and you can say you adopt it or you don't adopt. And then it is our opinion we don't need this, and we return this right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think -- speaking for myself, I think it's inappropriate that the Bench should read it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may something about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I start to feel a bit uncomfortable now, what is happening. I will read the document, but I can say already now I will -- I will not give any statement on that later on during this morning because I -- we never made any agreement during that meeting that this should happen. There was no recollection of that whatsoever. It was, as I stressed before, an informal meeting on the request of Mr. Karadzic, which I granted. I went over there. We had an informal discussion about many things that happened over there. I might have expressed certain opinions, but it was way outside this Tribunal. It was on his request, and I granted him that, I co-operated with that, but I made no notes, it was not official, so I'm not very willing to react on that statement whatsoever. I will read it, if you require me to do so, but I don't think it's very fair to require me to react on statements from more than one year ago, of which I do not have any note. It's different from what the notes and the things that happened in 1995 and which are official documents and official testimony that I did in 2007 and 2009. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is in agreement with you, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. The appropriate way for this to have been done was for an aide-memoire or a note to have been made immediately after the interview, and to have sent it to you then, and to see whether or not that accorded with your memory. And certainly speaking for myself, and I think for all the Bench, we take the view that Mr. Tieger's right about the inappropriate nature of this intervention. What we would ask you to do is to read the note. If there's anything in that note that you feel, of your own volition, you can agree to, then so be it. But if there isn't, then, equally, so be it. And we will wait until you've read it before any determination of any further action. Mr. Robinson, it's plainly not the proper way to deal with a note of an interview like this. This is a matter which should have been confirmed with the witness prior to his testimony. It's almost cross-examination by ambush, which is not very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, I'm not asking you to confirm whether you said this to me or not, only to confirm whether that is your view, whether what is written there is correct, and whether that was a doctrine that you pursued during your mission in Sarajevo. Now, I would like you to focus on paragraph 16 of your consolidated statement, in which you say the following. You have it with you, I mean your consolidated statement. Paragraph 16, you say: [In English] "We always went to the hospital, and especially to the morgues, to investigate the killed people. This was an integrated part of the procedure, and we checked, together with the Bosnian police, the number of the killed people." [Interpretation] Now I'd like to put to you a document attached by the OTP to your statement, which is 65 ter 14354 -- oh, no, I apologise, 14345, 65 ter. Can I please have that in e-court. It's a report of 18th of June, 1995, compiled by a UNMO. Just one moment, please. 14345. I think I misspoke the first time, so 14345. I apologise just for a second. It's a UNMO report of the 18th of June, 1995, in which the observers are reporting certain facts to their headquarters, and you will shortly see what is written therein. While we are waiting: Is it true that you did not have access to the hospital at all times?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite recall [sic] that. It might been that on certain occasions that we were not granted access to the hospital, but I do not have a real clear memory on what happened. It might have been true that on some occasions we were not allowed to get into the hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What document are you referring to, Mr. Karadzic? 14345, is that what we are looking at now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is a wrong number. Actually, I have a wrong number. I am looking for an UNMO report of the 18th of June, 1995. We are trying to rectify this mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, who introduced those restrictions? Who prevented you from going to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know from who came -- from who came those restrictions. But as I said before many in declarations, we always worked together with the Bosnian police, doing the investigation, and there were occasions which I can recall that due to the tense situation, that it was not very appropriate to go into the hospital when people were in surgery or when families were around, and then the Bosnian police told us that it was better not to go into the hospital on certain occasions. But we were always granted the permission to visit the morgue in case there were killed people. But I do not recall from whom the Bosnian police had the authority or had the directions to do so, but I do know that we had, as UNMOs, the direction not to be -- to insisting on doing things -- actions which were against the will of the Bosnian authorities. So we had to work together with them, so we -- on certain occasions, we could be a bit more persistent or insisting than on other occasions. It was a from-case-to-case scenario that we had to handle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll find this document later. Now, who instructed you to co-operate so closely with the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was my direct superior. That was the senior military observer in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, I'm not interested who imposes restrictions personally, but it seems that whenever you were prevented from going into hospital to inspect the wounded people, you were prevented by the Bosnian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know -- I said before I don't know who in the Bosnian authority was doing so, but we were advised in those cases not to do so. And it was also a matter of the hospital staff that requested us very strongly not to insist in going into the hospital in order to investigate whatever had happened. And as I've said before, it is a matter of co-operation that we said, We are not going to do that. So we followed the lines of either the Bosnian police or the hospital authorities. I don't know from whom they got their directions, and I didn't pay any attention to that on that moment in time because we had much other things to worry about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm more interested in hearing whether that was the Bosnian side, and that is what you confirmed. Can we now have Exhibit P1860, P1860. It's already in evidence. I would just like you to have a look at it. Page 1. This is page 1; is that right? And this is a report sent to the HQ. Can we now have page 12. Will you please look at the paragraph which begins: "UNMO team SW-2 carried out investigation ..." [In English] " ... origin approximate 300 mag. Difficult to confirm. Fragments removed by local CivPol, and impact was on the concrete ..." [Interpretation] And then it says: [In English] "... UNMOs were allowed to visit Kosovo hospital and the morgue where they could confirm seven were killed. They were informed that there were 10 injured casualties in the same incident. Comment: UNMOs have not been allowed to visit hospitals since 15th of June, and are still not allowed to do so, but in this case an exception was made." [Interpretation] Was that the sort of restrictions that were imposed during investigations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know. This is a report of a different UNMO team, so I cannot judge that. I don't know what happened exactly over there, I don't know what they encountered. I only can discuss the situation that I had with my own team. And as I stated before, on some occasions we were not allowed to visit the people that were wounded. We always were granted permission to visit the morgue. And I cannot comment upon the actions of the other UNMO teams. That's way out of my business. I don't know about it, so I have nothing to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that neither you nor anyone else from your team had the required training or experience for the purpose of establishing the time and cause of death; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I had no, neither had my people, specific medical training in order to -- we were no doctors or medical personnel, so we have no training or experience in exactly establishing time and cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what kind of criterion was to be applied in order to determine the freshness of a dead body? On the basis of what can you say that that was the body of a person killed recently?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The only thing I can say about that is that when a person is killed recently, as far as my experience over there recalls, is the fact that -- the stiffness of the body and the fact that blood or other -- I don't know how to recall that correctly - let's keep it on blood - is still pouring out, or coming out, or -- coming out of the body. That's a matter of judgement that you learn during the period. I fully admit that the first time I saw that, that I had no knowledge whatsoever, but, unfortunately, during six months in Sarajevo, and having seen on several occasions those bodies, you have an idea, but only just an idea formed, whether these people were killed a long time before or not, and I can give you no specifics whatsoever on that. It's a matter of judgement on the moment, having a feeling about. And as I said before, we were no medical experts and we had no medical experts in our teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If possible, can you please answer me with a yes or no. Did you ever carry out an external visual examination of a body stripped of the clothes, and did you provide a description of the wounds on the body?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever try to check whether there was rigour-mortise? Did you ever try to move the limbs of the body?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No. Sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know at which point rigour-mortise sets in and when it ceases to exist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to intervene, Mr. Karadzic. Speaking for myself, having heard you cross-examine the witness with patience, I'm at a loss where you're leading. Don't expect from us to extend your time for cross-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Another point, Dr. Karadzic, is: As you will know better than most, the question of when rigor-mortise sets in depends upon a huge number of variables, not the least of which is the ambient temperature, and so -- and this witness has already stated he has no medical expertise, so how can he help?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I just wanted to ask one more question; for example, if he ever touched any of the dead bodies to check the body temperature. And I know exactly where this is leading to. This is leading to the events after the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, have you ever established the body temperature by touching the corpse?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After you would receive information about an incident, you would go to the site, and in most cases the local police would have arrived there before you, is that correct, and it was the police who informed you about the casualties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, that's not the generic approach. In several cases, we met the local police on their police station, and we went together to the site of what had happened. So there was a variety of approaches. On some occasion the police was already there, and on some occasions, we were found -- we went to the police station and we picked up the local police and brought them in our car to the site of the incident, because the police had problems with their transportation, so we granted them transport in our cars. So there was a variety of approaches. The only thing that was fixed in that is that we always did the investigation together with members of the Sarajevo police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you drive police officers to the site, did it ever happen that you found any police officers already present on the scene? Can you look at the paragraph from your 2006 statement: [In English] "We would hear from the Bosnian police about casualties." [Interpretation] Paragraph 7, paragraph 7. Is it possible that the police had not arrived before you and the police officers that you were driving to the site, and that site was not secured by anyone? Is it possible that you were the first to arrive?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know that. That might have been, but I really don't know.
