I don't recall that, that amount of detail, whether any member of the police force was already there or not, because they were working in civilian and they were not recognisable when you came on the scene of an explosion. I really don't know that. I cannot give any proper answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the information about the victims you received from the Bosnian police, and it never happened that you actually found the victims at the scene ever; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: To begin with the last one, that's correct, but we always went together with the Bosnian police to the morgue or, on certain occasions, to the hospital in order to check the number of killed and wounded people. So that information we could confirm ourselves in counting the killed people inside the morgue. And we had to do so because that was our part -- part of our job, to offer an impartial opinion to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Important information you received from the Bosnian police, though. Do you know that we suspected these Bosnian police officers of staging incidents all around Sarajevo; yes or no? Are you aware that we publicly sought joint investigations and that we suspected precisely those police officers of planting incidents?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Again, I cannot answer all your questions with yes or no, so I would like to know: Who do you mean by "we suspected"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbian side. The Serbian Army asked to take part in the investigations. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For example, information about the fact that the line of separation is 1.050 metres away from Markale, did you get that from the Bosnian police or did you, yourself, establish that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I did not establish that, neither did I get that from my -- from the Bosnian police. That was information that was given to us by the -- and, again, I don't know whether it was exactly 1.050 metres, I don't recall that. But information on the confrontation line, the generic -- the generic outline of the confrontation line was given to me by the -- by my superiors, my military superiors, in the headquarters of the UNMOs in Sarajevo. I had no information on that by the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your investigations, you never determined the origin of fire, but only the place and the direction from where the projectile came?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I, myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're reading the interpretation. [In English] "But only the place -- not place but only the direction from where ..." [Interpretation] You did not establish the place from where the projectile was fired, but only the direction from where the projectile came; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 23 of the consolidated statement, you say the following, paragraph 23: [In English] "During the investigations which I conducted of shelling incidents, I tried to find the direction of fire, but never specifically traced the shell back to the actual point of origin. Not only was no time for that; more importantly, it was impossible to do so because informations on the charge ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Do you see that, that, that, that part? And then in the same paragraph, you say: [In English] "There are no UNMOs left position any more on the Serb side who were able to confirm outgoing fire." [Interpretation] You were thus unable to establish the responsibility for the incident. You could not establish which side was responsible for the firing of a specific shell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I, personally, and I explained that in my -- in various statements, could not do that. But I have to say that, to make it clear, what is happening, my piece of information that I recollected on the spot of the explosion was only a part of the total overall information that UNPROFOR or the UNMOs were collecting, so if you -- that's what we call military intelligence. You gather bits of pieces of information. One is the place of the explosion, one is the -- another one is the direction of fire, and the third one are other reports of outgoing rounds from various other UNMO or other UNPROFOR institutions. And by -- by combining those -- that information, which I could not do because I was stationed inside the city, so my piece of information was recollecting the grid of the -- the place of the explosion, plus the origin of fire, could give my superiors the opportunity to connect that information with the other information, and from there come to the conclusion where -- from which side the round came, either from Bosnian Army territory or from Bosnian Army-held territory. That is how military intelligence works. And UNPROFOR, and especially the UNMOs, were military people working with military intelligence and bringing together pieces of information which brings you to conclusions. But I fully admit that I was not able to do so on the basis of my own observations on the spot, on the scene of an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are saying that your findings, the information, your reports, were not enough, in the legal and criminal sense, to establish beyond a reasonable doubt who fired and from where; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm not saying anything in the legal or criminal sense. I reject those words, the use of those words. I don't know what they mean. My job as an UNMO was to establish the military situation inside the city of Sarajevo. That was my job. I stated that before, and that was in the SOP -- the standard operating procedure of the UNMOs. So what I had to do was to witness, to see, to write down, to report whatever was happening in my area of operations or even if I could see things outside that. It is not my job -- it was not my job to say anything about the legitimacy or the criminality of operations that took place on that moment in time. That was for my superiors to do. I had nothing to do with legitimacy or criminality in an operation on that moment. My job was to be an impartial United Nations Military Observer with the priority for the word "military observer." An observer means I had to observe. I had to make no judgement on the legitimacy or the criminality of an operation. So I really would not like to react on those words. I reject those words, because they were outside our scope of our working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you will admit that your statements are full of qualifications which have a certain legal criminal weight. The Serbs were disrupting, the Serbs were firing at random, the Serbs were firing areas that are civilian areas without military targets. Do we then have to look at what you said then, in light of what you have just stated now?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It's your interpretation that you interpret my words with having a certain legal and criminal weight. I only stated what I observed after six months of experience in Sarajevo. You cannot deny my words that I have seen projectiles falling on civilian targets. That's something you cannot deny from me. That's what I saw. I saw, on the 28th of August, what happened. I came not to the conclusion that that round came from the Serb side. That was a conclusion from the commander of UNPROFOR. So what I have stated, whether it has a legal weight or a criminal weight, or whatever you make of that, that has nothing to do with my statement. My statements are about what I saw and what I witnessed, without any form of legitimacy or idea about criminality. I saw, during six months, random firing inside the city of Sarajevo. Most of those rounds were coming from -- it was established, was confirmed, coming from the Serb side. Whether that's legal, whether there was a legal basis for that, that's not for me to judge. Whether it was criminal, it's not for me to judge. I only can say what I saw, what I witnessed, and what my team did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in paragraph 43 of the consolidated statement, state that each shell -- that every single round the Serb forces fired into the city frightened people, and that's what they wanted to -- frighten people -- [In English] " ... frighten people, and that's what they wanted, to frighten people." [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, here you're making a judgement. Did you ever discuss any Serb commander -- have a discussion with any Serb commander in order to establish why something was a target, why something was being fired at?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: To begin at the last one, I never discussed anything with any Serb commander. I was not on the Serb side. I was stationed inside the city. That's my first part of the answer. The second thing is it is again a fact that I witnessed. It is not a judgement. It is a fact that I witnessed. Six months' long, and it's connected to what I stated before, it is the fact that I saw that we - my team - I, myself, and my people, we witnessed falling rounds, especially mortar rounds, throughout the city in a random pattern, not in a way that you combat military targets with. It is not a judgement. It is a witness statement. It is what I witnessed during those periods. I don't know why the Serb commanders did it. I don't know what orders they had. I had no opportunity to talk with them. There has been no opportunity. I don't know what was in their minds, what their orders from their superiors were to do so. The fact is what I saw is that they were random firing with single rounds or a few rounds on areas where there were no military targets whatsoever, and that brought me to the judgement that I made or to the witness statement that I made. You may call it a judgement. That's up -- that's your conclusion. I call it those things that I witnessed, those things that I saw in the period that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come to that. In paragraph 21 of the consolidated statement, you say that in cases where you did not think that projectiles were fired from Serbian territory, that does not mean "it should not be presumed that we determined the fire came from the Bosnian Muslims." So if you had no evidence that it was the Serbs, you did not even think that it could have come from the Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct, because we never witnessed from my area any outgoing rounds from Muslim Army territory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D2837 in the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, you state, in the part that I quoted, that you know what the Serbs wanted, but you did not even wish to speak with the Serbian commanders. They wanted to frighten people, that, We wanted to frighten the civilians, both Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo; is that correct? But let's look the this document. This is SC-1. This is from your team; is that right? --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 2(a): "Lieutenant-Colonel Konings walked up along the path which leads to the actual OP. The total length of this path is about 200 metres. When Lieutenant-Colonel Konings had walked about 50 metres, a single 20-millimetre round was fired, somewhere from the top of the hill, into the city." [Interpretation] And then at C you say: [In English] "... came to the conclusion that these rounds seemed to have come from the BH side." "D. Major Jackson was on duty some 150 metres away in the OP. He confirmed the above-mentioned facts and had the same impression." [Interpretation] Is this opposite to what you said a bit earlier, that you had never seen fire from Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: This is a different situation. The situation we were discussing before was firing from Muslim territory on the city, itself. This is a fact that occurred where we had the impression that from the confrontation line, a 20-millimetre round was fired on our OP-1. So it's something differently, but it happened, and what's stated here is absolutely correct. It's our -- our recollection of what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here "into the city," not at your position. There is also references to fire at your positions in other documents. But it says "into the city." If you look at 3: "Before we could send -- [In English] " ... this increp, about 10 rounds SA were fired in the general direction of OP-1. The origin of fire was very clearly the top of the hill, some 200 metres south of the OP, which means that to the opinion of the UNMOs, these rounds came from the BH side." [Interpretation] Thus, there was fire at the city and also at your OP from the Muslim side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Our first impression at that moment, what I recall, is that the fire was aimed at our OP, just above our OP, and you cannot avoid that those rounds will carry on further and will hit a place in the city. Yes, I don't deny that. You're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D899, Your Honours. Sorry, Your Honours, I stand corrected, D889. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were aware that the UNMO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note we did not hear what Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters couldn't hear what you said. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from this, even in cases where you were not personally present, you had information that some other observers, military observers and representatives of the UN, had information, all saw that Muslim forces fired at the Muslim parts of the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the only information I heard. I never witnessed it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Captain Hansen was in the area where you were. He was the leader of the team before you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to look at your statement on page 2, the statement from 1996, page 2: [In English] "On May the 5th, 1995 --" [Interpretation] So Hansen was your predecessor, the team leader in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter -- this has a D number, 853, D853. D853.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the first page, and you can see that this is a report of the 28th of June: [In English] "A UNMO coming into the PTT building, parking his car on the lower parking place, observed the following: Heard and saw an outgoing projectile across the parking place and road from grid BP866587. The place is in the BH territory, approximately 1.800 metres from the nearest confrontation line. Dust was seen and a low-flying projectile heading toward the PTT building." [Interpretation] Is this one of the things that you heard or that you heard of?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't recall that in detail. I really -- I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the Muslim forces in Sarajevo -- other than what Captain Hansen is talking about, modified air-bombs, did you know that Muslims in Sarajevo had 107- and 128-millimetre rockets in Sarajevo and that they fired them?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I said before, I only can talk about the part of the city that I was working in and about the period that I was working there, and I have no information that in that part of the city they had these types of rockets and that they fired with those rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a little bit earlier, as well as in your statements, that Sarajevo was shelled at random, because, in your opinion, there weren't too many military targets there. Would you look at paragraph 26 of your statement from 2006, where you say [In English] "there are not too many military targets." [Interpretation] And in paragraph 27 of the consolidated statements, you say: "I never saw any real concentration of troops, although sometimes our movement was impeded by Bosnian roadblocks ." Do you see those two paragraphs, paragraph 26 on page 6, from 2006, and paragraph 27 in the consolidated statement? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I hope you give me some time to read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the consolidated statement, could you please look at 31 and 33, where you talk about the presence of soldiers in town and about their grouping?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would allow me to read first paragraph 27, and then I will take care of the other paragraphs as well. Thank you. And which were the other paragraphs that you wanted to read me? 31, 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, let's look at 27. You had movement restrictions, and this could have -- did this have an effect on your ability to gain insight into the situation in the city, in terms of the numbers, the weaponry, the installations, and so on in the town?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, the restrictions of movement inside the city were not as such that they prohibited us to do our work properly. We had -- from time to time, we had moments or even sometimes a day of restriction of movement, but inside the city, itself, inside the part that I was responsible for, with the exception of permission to go into the confrontation line, we had enough opportunity to get a clear view of the amount and number and sort of troops that were -- that were in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at 31 and 33, please. "There were soldiers in the city but not in big groupings. There were single soldiers or lone police officers, but Sarajevo was not a militarised city." [Interpretation] Was Sarajevo demilitarised? Was it a demilitarised town?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I just say that there was a low number of small troop combinations or troop organisations present in the city. I haven't ever anything said about whether it was a demilitarised city or such a city. I only said it didn't look very militarised. I might -- I used that term in order to explain that I didn't see large forces inside my part of the city. As I explained, they occurred -- only they worked in small groupings, single soldiers. There were no heavy weapons systems present. We didn't see any, let's say, lines of defence, typical military preparations for larger combat operations there. And, again, I can't -- to repeat it, the use of the word "militarised" is to explain as such, that it looked very civilian, with most only civilians on the streets and a very low number of military troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that the town was practically of a reduced ability for defence and that the Serbs could have captured it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's your conclusion. I never -- I cannot state that. I only can judge my part of the city. I cannot stress that over and over again. I have no idea about the number of Bosnian troops in other parts of the city. In my part of the city, there were very few Bosnian troops. I stated that before. I don't know how many troops were in the confrontation line because, again, we were not granted access to that. I had no information on that. So the conclusion that the Serbs could have captured Sarajevo, that's your conclusion. It's not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I tried to draw that conclusion from your position. Please look at your statement from 2006, paragraph 3 on page 2: [In English] "Having seen the strength of the Muslim forces inside the city, I think it would have been a brutal and bloody fight." [Interpretation] So in 2006, you were making a military estimate that in view of the Muslim forces in the city, a battle to take the city would be brutal and bloody; correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my statement of that time, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence shall tell you, Lieutenant-Colonel, that in your zone, where you were observing, three brigades were active, three Muslim brigades; 105th Mountain Brigade, 151st Mountain Brigade, and 115th Mountain Brigade, around 15.000 soldiers. Only one brigade had 6.000 soldiers. Do you know that in the area you observed, there were three active brigades?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I recall some of these numbers, especially the 105th, I think, but I'm not quite sure. But, well, if you say that they had so much soldiers, if I -- if I count them together, 15.000 soldiers, I'm not quite sure whether these 6.000 belonged to the 15.000 or that I have to add these to the 15.000, but I can only state once more that I never have seen much soldiers on the street. If you put in the small area that I was operating in, because it's a rather small area of the city, it's a very compressed area, if you put there more than 15.000 soldiers, I'm quite sure we should have noticed that and we should have seen them moving around or even should have seen fortifications of places where they were -- where they were putting their people together, where they were bringing their people together. I think -- we never saw that amount of soldiers in there. So if you say so, that they were there, that's your opinion. I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know, Lieutenant-Colonel, that up to 75 per cent of the Muslim soldiers, according to their own documents, waged war in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I haven't seen those documents, so I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Legal Officer for the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have behind you, Witness, a map of the city with the zones of responsibility of these three brigades marked on it. Could the copies please be distributed to the parties. And the document, based on which these markings were made, is a Muslim document, 1D2839. We can call it up in e-court, and we will view the map on paper. Could a photocopy also be given to Mr. Konings. While we are waiting, Lieutenant-Colonel: Do we agree that on the front-line, on the forward line, one normally does not keep artillery, or mortars, or communication centres, or headquarters, or logistical bases?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I will not agree with you, because it depends on, first of all, what do you mean with "forward line." Secondly, I'm quite sure that in any forward line, you will find mortars, you will find communication, you will find certain headquarters. You will not find logistical bases. But it all depends on which level you are talking about. It depends on the operational level that you are discussing. Is it a tactical level, the operational level? Are you talking about platoons, are you talking about brigades? It's a very generic question that I cannot agree with, unless you explain me exactly what you -- what you are talking about so that I can try to share an opinion or offer you an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a look at the paper before us. Do you know that each section of the city was covered by the area of responsibility of one of the brigades? Look at Brigade 115. Its area of responsibility is from the confrontation line to the Miljacka River. You can look to your right. There is a map in colour.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document we have is, unfortunately, without translation, but still we should look at page 3. Three brigades are described there that were active in the old town. 115th Brigade organises and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You referred to 65 ter 1D2839, which is not this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a document of the 12th Division Command that was active in the city of Sarajevo, itself, and it's an order for blocking defence from the 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether we have a 65 ter number for this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have one for the map. This city plan is based on this document. The data is in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that map was produced by the Defence team allegedly based upon information which is contained in this document; that's what you're saying, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this document of the 12th Division of the Muslim Army, there are three brigades in the city, the 115th, the 152nd, and 105th. These three brigades were active in the area of observation of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand. I would like to advise you, then, to put your case to the witness to see whether he can help us in this regard, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, it is the case of the Defence that the 105th Brigade had at least 5.000 men, if not more, that its area of responsibility was from Vrdonje [phoen], Streliste, Klade Vode [phoen], up to Lepevir [phoen], where they boarded with another brigade. The 105th Brigade also had an area of responsibility up to the center of town, and the 152nd Brigade had a zone of responsibility from down-town to Colina Kapa, up to Miljacka River. Now, the deployment of all these soldiers, the headquarters of all these companies, battalions, et cetera, their communications centres, their artillery and mortar support, and their routes for manoeuvre, for food supply, and munitions supply, and daily movements of units and rotations, which you said you observed at least for one of these brigades, this area of the city, your area, was completely militarised with a huge number of legitimate military targets that formed the infrastructure of three large brigades. How come you were not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I -- the simple factor is there that I -- I know that there were three so-called brigades in that area, and I even recall the numbers, and I do not deny their areas of operations as they are on the map, although I do not recollect the exact borders of their area of responsibility, as we call it. But if you are starting to talk about - and I refer to what you said before - headquarters of all these companies, battalions, their communication centre, their artillery and mortar support, their route for manoeuvre for food supply, munitions supply, daily movements of units and rotations, I haven't seen anything, as such. And if I recollect to my own memory the movement of a brigade, and we're talking about a brigade, you talk about 5.000 soldiers in an area that's rather small. It's a compressed area. It's only a few kilometres by a few kilometres, and I know, for 99.9 per cent, with my experience and my recollection of what a brigade actually is, if you put 5.000 people, and I even think three times 5.000 people, in my area of operations with, what Mr. Karadzic says, communications centre, artillery and mortar support, food supply, munitions supply, I would be the greatest fool of the world, and my team including, if we wouldn't have noticed that, and we haven't noticed that. We haven't seen anything, as such. The brigade commanders that I met -- I met the commanders of those three brigades. The brigade commanders I met were young majors. At least they called themselves "major." And they were talking about commanding a few hundred people. So I don't know where the truth is. I only can say that I did not see large troop movements, I did not see ammunition supply, I did not see -- you have to think. When you have a unit of 5.000 people, 5.000 soldiers in an area of a few kilometres, you will see them. If they supply themselves, you will see it, you will notice it. We haven't seen it. So if they were there, they did an excellent job in camouflaging themselves. I can say that. I can give them the best credit I can give, as a military professional, then they were hiding very, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perfectly correct. In their orders they say explicitly, Take every measure possible to prevent the UNPROFOR from gaining insight into the situation on our terrain. Is this document accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's proper to admit this document through this witness. You'll have another opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up 1D2567 to see how they managed to conceal it all from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, these brigades, according to their information, had a strength of 12.000 to 15.000, depending on how many they transported out of the city and how many were brought in. Can we look up page 6 of this document. Look at the first page first. It's the 11th of June, when you were there. Look under "Anti-Armour Combat." That's paragraph 7. We need the same in English. That must be the next page. "Only for anti-armour combat." Look at the task. First of all, look at the rocket batteries. Velesici, granted, is outside your zone, but look at this: "Prevent the enemy, armoured and mechanised units, from penetrating along the axes accessible to tanks ..." Et cetera, et cetera: "Organise POP-12, a platoon of tanks and an armoured platoon in the area of Ciglane." And then you see POP-3 in the area of Sedrenik. Look at all this activity of the armour and the launchers in your area. Page 8, please -- page 10 in English, to see how they prevented you from seeing what was going on. It says: "Establish a special traffic regimen with maximum control of vehicles and persons; in particular, those of the UNPROFOR, the UNMOs, and other international organisations." Did you find it? It's the fourth bullet point from the bottom: "If necessary, close all access routes and exits from Sarajevo for UNPF and other international associations. Ban all representatives of international institutions from entering the combat zone without special authorisation of the 12th Division of the Land Forces commander. Prevent the UNPF from pulling out and encircle them if necessary. Prevent photography and documentation." So they're taking maximum efforts to camouflage themselves, and they are launching a massive offensive operation from the city, itself. And, of course, I understand the camouflage was successful and managed to deceive you, but how do you see this situation now, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Karadzic, I totally disagree with you. I'm still convinced -- and I meant that sarcastically what I said before, that they did a perfect job in camouflaging themselves. I am convinced, as a professional soldier, that once you launch an offensive including 15.000 troops, you will not be able to hide that in a city. We would have seen that. And we had not such restriction of movement that we were not able to drive around and to see military equipment or to see so-called assembly areas which you establish before you start an attack. You will not be able, in such a compressed environment as Sarajevo, as such is, to hide or to conceal such large massive amount of troops. If they already had them, I don't know. I cannot read the documents. I don't know how the troops were built up. I had no information on that on that moment, and I don't have it now. I only can say that to my recollection, to my opinion, it is just not possible to launch a massive offensive operation from the inner of a city without being noticed by anybody. That's just impossible. You cannot hide track vehicles, tanks, and whatever you -- what is assumed that the Muslims had, you cannot hide that in that area with small streets, with -- it's just not possible without being noticed either by us, the UNMOs, or by other UNPROFOR troops in that area. So whatever you bring in -- in front of me, I haven't seen these documents before. It's fine, they describe the situation as it has been established from I think it's 12th Division or the 12th Corps; I don't know. I only can offer you my opinion, and that's what I've done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do not dispute, Lieutenant-Colonel, that the Muslim Army had prepared and started the first offensive of the 1st of May, and intensified it on the 15th, they took advantage of the fact that we were busy with air-strikes in the end of May - I'm speaking on behalf of your UN documents - and launched another new offensive on the 1st of June. Would you deny that the UN reported on this major offensive originating from the city of Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know what the UN reported, neither on the 1st, because I was not in Sarajevo on that moment. I don't know what they reported on the 15th or later in May. I only know what I reported, myself, and what my direct superiors reported, because what the UN reported - and I don't know what you mean by the UN - either the UN in command of UNPROFOR or the UN in New York, I really don't know, but we were -- we had no access to that information whatsoever. I had my only information from my direct superior, because we had no radio communication with the outside world. I had no radio or television, so I did not know what the UN outside Sarajevo was reporting or even doing, so I cannot add anything to this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise, there's no basis for this document to be admitted through this witness. You will have another opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, your mission, as I quoted from your evidence in the Milosevic case, was to report on military developments in the city, and the most important task was to be an impartial witness of the UNPROFOR inside the city of Sarajevo and to provide reports on every incident -- every happening that occurred in the city. So you were an eye-witness for the UNPROFOR, and you should know what those three brigades were doing in your area. P1860 is the document we need next. It's a sitrep. Would firing incidents in your area of observation be something you would have to report on?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. This is from the 19th of June, an UNMO report forwarding a report they got from you in amalgamated form. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: No, I reject the idea. I don't know. You don't tell me what you are aiming at, so I would really appreciate that you highlight what you are -- what you are really aiming at. This is not a report what they got from me. This is a report from HQ Zagreb to the UN. It has nothing to do with my team. So would really appreciate if you make clear whatever you want to state or what you want to ask of me, because I get really confused, while being confronted with documents that are none of my business, that were none of my business. I was not working at the UNMO HQ in Zagreb. I was a military observer inside a small part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would be patient. You will see that it is relevant, it is related to you. Look at this sentence in line 2: [In English] "Limited B and H offensive, I expected to continue." [Interpretation] "Limited ABiH offensives are expected to continue." Can we now see page 8? Is it 8?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt once more. I didn't see line 2, what you are -- what you are aiming at? Which line 2? Is that now in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Top of the page on the screen, if you are looking at e-court.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I read that. But what has that to do with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It just says that it's expected that the offensive of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which started on the 15th of June, is expected to continue. Now, if we look at page 8, we'll see the inputs for this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to intervene for the benefit of the witness. I think it's fair enough for the witness to say so. I asked you to put your case to the witness first. What is your question? Ask the question and, if necessary, put the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is our case that on the 15th of June, from the city of Sarajevo, an offensive of enormous scale started against the Serbian territories around Sarajevo, and the United Nations were aware of it, and that the brigades inside your area of observation were fully participating in that offensive and fired from the city. And we see on this page, in line 4, "SC-1," that you even observed some of that fire and reported it. And towards the bottom, there's another incident recorded at 1300 hours. The first one was at 1130.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would really appreciate if we also would look to the grids that the originating fire came from. And if you have an offensive going on, if you have a battle going on between two warring factions or between two armies, whatever you call it, it is logical that both armies use their weapons systems, whether they are the Serbs or whether they are the Bosnian Army. If there is an offensive from the Bosnian Army, and I do not deny that, which is quite obvious in a struggle -- in a war that's going on, that both parties either do offensive or defensive operations, which is normal military logic, and it's normal that both parties use a variety of weapons systems. That we reported outgoing rounds, as stated here, I do not deny that, but it would also be interesting to look to a certain -- to the grids that were established on that moment. So, yes, there were a few outgoing rounds, but four rounds in a time-scale between 1130 and 1300 hours can hardly be known or be seen as a massive offensive operation. If I recall a massive offensive operation, and I have seen them around Sarajevo, but then it was concentrating on the confrontation line, all the firing was going on around the confrontation line, not from the inside of the city to the outskirts. And, again, four rounds -- four outgoing mortar rounds do not recall to me as being a massive -- a major offensive operation, really not. It's something that happened. I do not deny that, and I would be interested to see where the Grid BP941618 is, whether it's inside the city or outside the city. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you did report this. Can we now have 1D1842 -- correction, 1D2842. Now, look at the report on the 105th Brigade of the 18th of June. There were 483 rounds of fire, not counting bullets; only the mortars that explode on impact. There is an English version available as well. Then you have "RPG," and then you have "154 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters have difficulty following you. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So starting from grenade launcher 9, 95 pieces, downwards until number 15, which is from 7 to 15, the total is 483 firing rounds from the area of one brigade alone, and that brigade was in your view. Would you consider that an insignificant fire? This is the document produced by the Muslim side, and they are reporting, actually, the consumption of ammunition by the brigade.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, in itself, it doesn't say anything about how and where and when these ammunitions were used, and in relation to what. It's just a number of rounds that apparently were used in a certain situation. And if that is connected to an offensive operation from any army, that seems to me to be very logical, because if you do an offensive operation, you use your weapons system, so you use ammunition. That's even applicable up until today when we do operations in Afghanistan, where we use a substantial amount of ammunition when doing an offensive operation. So the number doesn't say me anything. It doesn't say me where they came from, why they were used, against whom they were used, where they were fired from, so it's a number, nothing more, nothing less, for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the area of responsibility of the 105th Brigade. From this area, but definitely not from the front-line, but rather from the depth of its zone, they fired at the Serbian positions 485 times. So they're not firing from the front-line, they're firing from in-depth into the territory, and one should say that such huge fire cannot be effected from the front-line. It has to be down behind the lines. Look how many mortars were fired, and that was fire support for an infantry attack. Artillery and mortar fire support, followed by an attack, and the UN in Sarajevo knew about this very well. Is this correct, Lieutenant-Colonel? So we are not talking about four grenades only. We are talking about a variety of shells of different calibres?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Again, I only can see a list in front of me where -- apparently by -- this is a report of the Bosnian Army, where they claim to have fired a certain amount of rounds in order to support an attack. That's what I assume. These rounds, when you refer that to the 105th Brigade, which is practically -- which is in the middle of my area of operations, were not fired from the inner circle of that area; absolutely not. I don't know where they fired them from. Probably close from the confrontation line in an area where we were not allowed, but they were not fired from the built-up area that the most -- the biggest part of the 105 Brigade is located and that we had a vision to and that we had allowance to move around. So 483 rounds of larger calibre would have been noticed and would have been reported. That's -- that's a very clear thing. We would not miss them in order to do so. And, again, this is a report about a certain use of ammunition. It's logical that a brigade that does an attack uses a certain amount of ammunition, but I already explained that before, what my opinion is about that, so I have nothing to add to that further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 34 of your consolidated statement, you say: [In English] "There was a battle at the confrontation line, there may have been something close to equal fire, but it was hard to count rounds during such battles and hard to determine who was firing. We had no proper equipment to see a source of fire; only binoculars, until they were stolen. Only by doing a site investigation could we determine direction of fire." [Interpretation] So this is an outgoing fire that you failed to notice and which you did not report. Do we have a reason not to trust their report, in which the brigade, itself, is reporting how many rounds of ammunition were used, which was an obligation of the commander, Major Izet Berkovac, to do so?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: First of all, I deny what you're saying. This outgoing fire, I don't know exactly what you mean by that, but we did not miss 483 rounds. I stated that before. There were no 483 outgoing rounds from the specific area of 105 Brigade. There were a lot of fighting going on during those days in the confrontation line. There were many explosions in the confrontation line, so many that we were not able to count it or even to make note of from where they came or from whom they were. That was a visualisation of the fact that there was a huge battle going on in and around the confrontation line. But as I stated before, we were not allowed close to the confrontation line, due to various factors. It was much too dangerous there, and it was an ordered to stay away from that, especially on those days when there was a lot of fighting going on. But on those occasions, there were not 483 large caliber rounds outgoing from the area of 105 Brigade. I don't know what I can make more clear of that. So we did not miss them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Due to the shortage of time, sir, we're not showing the daily consumption. Starting from the 15th of May until the 15th of July, thousands of shells were fired, and not less than 1.000 shells were fired from your area by these brigades from the depth of their territory, and this area, Lieutenant-Colonel, was full of legitimate military targets. Are you trying to say that these forces were not structured in the similar way as the JNA or NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- Dr. Karadzic, with respect, is getting argumentative with the witness and giving evidence, himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought he was giving his case to the witness, and the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what I can add to it more. What I already stated is that the large amount of outgoing rounds from the depth -- what Mr. Karadzic called the depth of the brigade area of operations, they were not. We haven't witnessed so many rounds. That's absolutely what I can state. During the period that I was there, that's one thing I can say. The second thing, I can only repeat what I have already stated, I think, 10 times before, is that we did not witness the amount of troops that is now scheduled to be there -- to have been there, and I don't believe that 15.000 Bosnian Army troops were in the specific part of Sarajevo that I was doing my work; especially mounting a large attack from such a small area, and I said it before, to my opinion, it is, first of all, nearly impossible; secondly, if it would have been done, we would have seen it, especially during clear daylight, because it was partly happening during clear daylight. So I just do not believe in that. I cannot add anything more to what I already said, and I start to repeat myself, and I don't think you are waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to take a break, Mr. Karadzic. Do you like to tender that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The witness commented on this document, and we need that to understand his context. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D890, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour. We'll resume at 10 past 2.00. At that time, Mr. Karadzic, you will have an hour to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Ten past 1.00, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 10 past 1.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson, we received the response from Mr. Tudjman, and I read your motion for reply, but I was wondering whether you could agree to the method suggested by Mr. Tudjman or, in one way or another, come to a sort of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have a solution in mind which is a little bit different; that is, to ask the Government of Croatia whether it would waive the state's secrets requirement, so that it would allow him to be interviewed by us. So we prefer to be the ones to conduct the interview. And if you would allow us to submit a reply, we could submit it today, and it covers our proposal for trying to resolve that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We go back to open session, and we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the witness, I have to say the following: This witness cannot be validly questioned during the remainder of the time that I have. I have to question him about the Markale, the sniping incident, the air-bombs, et cetera, and there are lots of things that pertain to the zone of the three brigades that he observed. UNPROFOR said, anyway, that these reports by the observers were unreliable. His statement is full of assertions, but, nevertheless, we have to deal with Markale, the sniping incident, and the air-bombs. And for that purpose, I kindly ask the Chamber to grant me one day more tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is simply your fault not to be able to cover what you deem important, after having spent two hours which, in the opinion of the Chamber, speaking for myself, at least, could have been put in 10 minutes. You have one hour, Mr. Karadzic. In the meantime, for your information, tomorrow, due to an extraordinary plenary of the Judges, we'll resume -- we'll start at quarter past 11.00, and we'll have two 90-minute sessions with a half-an-hour break. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, I don't think I wasted time, and the reason is that this witness's statement is full of assertions that the Defence has to comment and shed light on, and there's nothing else that I can do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do not waste time. Let's come to your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact is that I cannot finish. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Lieutenant-Colonel, whenever possible, would you please give me a yes-or-no answer. You participated in the investigation of the incident of the 28th of August which took place at Markale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived at the scene some 30 or 40 minutes after the incident, alongside investigators from the Bosnian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I came together there with the team of the Bosnian police, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the scene you found there was one of evacuation that was in progress of the dead and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: When I arrived on the scene, all the dead or wounded were already evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That means that the police -- the Bosnian police was already there and they had conducted certain operations before your arrival; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no evidence of that, but I assume that seeing the amount of people, that some of those people were Bosnian police. But I do not have any evidence of that. I arrived there together with a team of Bosnian police officers that I picked up at their police station. I'm not aware of who was walking around there. I don't know all the individuals that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of the documents, it is said that you arrived at the scene at around 11.55; is that correct? It's document P14445, a UN report: [In English] "The BH chief of police requested the UNMO assistants to investigate the incident. A team Sedrenik PTL arrived at the scene at 11.55 and was included along with sector engineer and BH police investigators as part of a joint investigation team." [Interpretation] Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether -- is this a document I have on the screen? Is that the document that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document is in evidence, but we don't have time to call it up. It's P1445, page 9. The parties can see it. But you do confirm that you arrived at around 11.45?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I confirmed what I said before, that I arrived around 40 minutes later than the impact. The impact was at 11.10, so I might have been there at 11.45 or 11.50. I really don't know that anymore. If there is an official report which you apparently refer to which has been put into evidence, I refer to P14445 [sic], it says "1.55," it might be as close as it can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you were not able to conduct the usually investigation at Markale and to apply the normal standards that are used in other investigations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That is not true. I did exact -- we used the exact same way of working as we did at any other investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 13 of your 2006 statement. Paragraph 13: [In English] "The term the 'fuse funnel,' on a hard surface such as the Markale incident, the fuse is often destroyed, leaving no funnel. At Markale, on the 28th of August, 1995, I did not see a fuse funnel." [Interpretation] And then you go on to say that the casualties had been evacuated. And in paragraph 53 of your consolidated statement, you say: [In English] "Forty minutes after the explosion, all the victims were evacuated." [Interpretation] Is it standard practice to change the scene of crime to such an extent, and is it possible, under such circumstances, to conduct an appropriate and proper investigation?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I said before, we did exactly the same sort of investigation as we did at any other investigation, so I do not know what you mean by "changing the scene of crime to such an extent" and -- I really don't know. I can only say, once more, we did exactly the same investigation as we did on every other occasion, which means trying -- establishing what happened, mortar explosion, find the line of fire, find parts of the mortar projectile, et cetera, et cetera, establish what we could see over there, remnants of bodies, which is, at the end, consolidated in my patrol report, which is, as part of the evidence of the OTP, of course, available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in your 2006 statement, paragraph 22, you, yourself, admitted that you conducted a limited investigation because none of you were expert in ballistics and you didn't have enough time or proper conditions for an investigation. [In English] "... it would have been easier later on, with real crater analysis experts with lots of time. I did not go back later on to the further measurement." [Interpretation] Is this what it says here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Which is exactly the same what we did every time. We never had time to do an extensive crater analysis. We never went back to any other sort of investigation. We kept it to a simple method, and the simple method is the limited investigation, that you try to establish, as good as you can, the line of fire and try to find the remnants of the mortar or any other projectile that was used. That is a limited investigation. And if you have more time and if you have the possibilities with instruments and -- survey instruments available, and if you have time, and if you are granted the possibility, and if it's not dangerous, you can do a lot of more things. But we did not have those instruments, we had only limited capabilities, so that's what we did over and over again. So this investigation was no exception to the rule, it was no exception in comparison with the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that for evacuation of 38 dead people and some 60 wounded people, at least twice as many people are required, and that all these casualties were evacuated by being loaded onto the trucks? Do you agree that such a high activity could have resulted in the tampering of the scene before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't agree with your statement. I don't know what happened in the time that I -- before I was there. I have no knowledge of that. I was not there, so I only can talk about the moment that I arrived and what I did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 76 of your consolidated statement, you said that one could roughly determine the origin of fire of the projectile; is that correct? [In English] " ... gives you the rough bearing of where the projectile came from."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: And which part are you -- which paragraph, 76?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 76: "The middle line of these two equal patterns gives you the rough bearing of where the projectile came from."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's correct, and later on I explained, in the same -- in this same explanation, what I meant with "rough bearing," because a compass reading is never exactly correct until the single minute or even what kind of measurement you use. It's still a compass bearing which is influenced by other external issues. That's what I mean with "a rough bearing."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you said that a mistake was possible. First of all, you said that you didn't use an army compass; secondly, that metal part of equipment could have affected the performance of the compass; and, thirdly, you listed a number of scenarios of the possible mistake and error. In your view, expressed in degrees, how big the mistake was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I express that in my report, and I think I stated there between 10 degrees left and 10 degrees to the right, which means that when you measure 170, the angle of fire could have been 180 or 160, but they are still -- are in a rough southern direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is correct that you did say that in one statement. This is the consolidated statement. Look at your statement, paragraph 15 of your statement from 2006. Paragraph 15: [In English] "We had to work very quickly because of the situation, the angry crowd, the need to complete our report as soon as possible. I'm sure that the margin of error could not have been 70 degrees difference, but it is possible that there may have been 30 to 40 degrees margin of error." [Interpretation] 5 to 45 degrees error of margin is possible according to your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I redirected that in my later statement, my amalgamated statement, until -- to 10 left and 10 right, so in a 20 of maximum, so that's all I can add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that no one from your team, including yourself, spoke with the eye-witnesses?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: We did not speak with any eye-witness, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you did not use a stick, even though the findings would have been more accurate with the stick?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I assume you refer to the stick method that you can use in order to measure the angle of fire. It's very hard to use sticks in a concrete environment, where you have no equipment for that. Besides that, we were not provided by the UN with sticks or any other equipment in order to measure the line of fire, so the thing we did, and I think that's accurate enough, is to divide the crater in two parts, two equal parts, and measure the line that you have on that by -- with a compass. It's the exact same method that the French UNPROFOR soldiers on the spot used, and they came, by the way, to the exact same direction of fire as we did, only they measured it in mils, which is a military method, and they came, I think, to 2.850 mils, which equals 170 degrees. That was our conclusion, so -- which is, apparently, that the line of fire was reasonably clear, that it came from the southern direction from the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the stabiliser was found at the scene. Can you tell us, what was the distance from the center of the explosion that the stabiliser was found?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure anymore. I think I've stated that somewhere in one of the reports. I think I used the term 10 metres, 10 or 15 metres, but I'm not quite sure. I should have to look that into my former declarations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will remind you. In paragraph 56 of the consolidated statement, you said 20 metres, and in the statement of 1996, on page 3, you said perhaps 50 metres from the center of the explosion. Is that right? And then in 2003, you said that it lay on the ground five to ten metres from the point of impact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: If these declarations are in my statements, then that's what I stated in that moment in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who took the stabiliser away from the scene, according to your information? Who took it away?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know who took it. I did not take it, so -- I don't know who took it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 10117, 10117. You have that document in front of you. That is your -- that is information, information report of the 3rd of September, 1993 -- 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you switch into e-court from Sanction. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3: [In English] "Konings recalls observing the tail-fin which was lying on the ground only five, ten metres from the impact." [Interpretation] How can you explain the difference between five metres and forty metres?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I cannot explain that at this moment in time. Those declarations have been taken from me in various moments in time, in 1996, in 2003, in 2006, and I hope you understand that bringing the memories back from that day in 1995 might cause some misunderstanding in where I found the tail and how much distance that was from the point of explosion. One thing, to make clear, we found the tail, and it was in the vicinity of the explosion. We explored the tail, and we saw -- we explored that it came from a 120-millimetre projectile. But I do not recall the exact distance anymore. And, again, those moments were taken in various moments of my further life after 1995, and I cannot explain why I used different distances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure that this is the right document. Can we have 65 ter 10120, 10120. 10120, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who took the stabiliser from the scene?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I said before, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can look at the first paragraph here, one sentence but last, where it says the video view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you know what document this is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a document in front of me, which is one of my declarations that I gave, and, yes, I think I have the right document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this is a report from the Prosecution after having an interview with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I read there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here: "The Special Committee of Inspectors of the Bosnian police ..." [In English] " ... collected the tail-fin. The tail markings of each round were verified and recorded by Higgs and for the UNMO reports." [Interpretation] Is that correct? Thus, the Muslim police took the tail-fin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have declared that in this report in 2003, so, yeah, well, I am -- on that moment, I declared it, so it must be correct. I do not really recall that today anymore. It's -- but if it's there -- if it says there I have said that, I have signed it, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that it wasn't unusual for the tail-fin to be so damaged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know where I said that, but you might show me that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 57 of the consolidated statement states that: "It wasn't unusual for the tail-fin to be bent." [In English] "It was not something unusual. On earlier occasions, we found tail-fins which were also damaged."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Do you know how this damage came about?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I explained in my report towards the Office of the Prosecution, it's that there's a huge force coming free once a projectile hits the ground and explodes, and that damage is -- that force is damaging the tail of the mortar projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that such a shell, with a charge that is bigger than the usual one, it is more common for the tail-fin to embed itself in the center of the explosion rather than to be ejected at some distance from the place of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "such a shell with a charge that is bigger than the usual one." I have no idea what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that. If this was a common bend of the tail-fin, why did you say that it had been driven over by a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the question. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually don't follow the one before that, either, Your Honour, where, at page 88, line 16, Dr. Karadzic asked Lieutenant-Colonel Konings: "What do you mean --" Or perhaps it was an answer: "-- by such a shell with a charge that is bigger than the usual one." I -- I've just -- where does that come from? I saw no reference to any statement by Lieutenant-Colonel Konings anywhere to that effect. And, similarly, I see no reference to where the second question is derived from, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You should give your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will come back to that, but it is generally known that the position of Lieutenant-Colonel Konings is that the shell of 120 millimetres is not fired with the basic charge, not even with the first charge, and that this one came with a charge greater than three, whereby it would have to be embedded into the ground, as it was in the Markale incident, for a distance of 26 millimetres -- centimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your statement. But before that: Mr. Konings, do you like to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because in the question or the remarks - I don't know whether I should call it a question or remarks - that are put forward now, different issues are now compared to each other, which make it impossible for me to answer questions. We are talking about a projectile tail. We are suddenly talking about the charge, but I assume that Mr. Karadzic means the charge that the projectile is fired with, not the charge that -- in the projectile body, itself. So suddenly a variety of parameters is coming in which I cannot comment upon. And I need to have clear questions on clear things, otherwise I cannot give you any clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but for that, we need more time. That is why we're hurrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 3 of your information report from 2003, where you say -- where the Prosecution interprets that you say: [In English] "the tail-fin was bent. While this is common as the effect of the blast normally damages the fins, the appearance of the tail-fin on the video suggests that it may have been damaged by vehicle tyres when the victims were moved."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: In which declaration are you reading that? I'm trying to find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably it's before -- on the monitor. Where is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The first paragraph on the screen: "A video view of the tail-fin also gives the impression it may have been damaged by tyre when the victims were --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see what you mean. It is a possible explanation, but what I -- it's important not to take that out of its proportions, is what I say before and what we say in relation to all other investigations that we did, is that the tail, nevertheless, is damaged. You find a damaged tail. The fact that the fins are completely bent, if you look to the video screen and looking to the movie, they are nearly folded against the body of the mortar projectile -- of the fin -- of the tail-fin, gave, at the moment that I saw the video, the impression that there might have been extra damage by tyres of a vehicle that drove on top of it, but that's just an assumption. I want to make clear that the tail of a mortar projectile of these types of mortars is damaged anyhow when it hits -- when it's hitting the ground and is part of the impact and part of the explosion. And that's what we found, a variety of damage to these fins, on all occasions that I did an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are assuming that the vehicles had driven over the tail-fin. How can we know where the tail-fin was, then, and what the scene was like before you got there? In other words, does that make it more difficult to establish what, actually, the situation was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, this question, with all due respect, is -- I'm the wrong person to ask that. I came there on a certain moment in time. I have established what I saw, I've written my patrol report. That's part of your evidence of my -- of the evidence in court. There are two patrol reports. Everything I've stated is there. In addition, there are several reports that were made in the period afterwards. And whatever happened before I came there, whatever has been done, I don't know. I only can state of what I saw and what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Markale I incident, the shell of the same calibre, 120 millimetres, that tail-fin embedded itself in the very center of the blast, on a similar surface, and it was embedded to a depth of 26 centimetres. Actually, the depth was nine centimetres below level zero. How do you explain that the tail-fin here was ejected so many metres away, whereas in the first case the tail-fin struck or was embedded in the very center of the blast?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no comment on the first Markale incident. I have no detailed knowledge of that, whatsoever, so I cannot comment on that. I only can comment on the things I saw and my explanation of what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that -- in paragraph 87 of the consolidated statement, you said: [In English] "Sarajevo was surrounded by Serb troops, and also in the biggest part around Sarajevo, Bosnian Army troops were opposing Serb troops in trenches. And in other military emplacements, there were various troops from both sides in the area between 170 degrees and 220 up to 240 degrees." [Interpretation] You are aware that in this range of these five shells were -- in that area, the Bosnian Army and Serbian Army troops were deployed?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that that morning it was quite clear and calm, and that is why you could hear the incoming fire, and had the fire -- had it been fired also from the Muslim territory, one would have been able to hear that as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: It's not only about the incoming fire; it's also about what I stated, the outgoing round, so the firing -- the actual firing of a projectile, itself. Everything that was in the vicinity -- in the larger vicinity of OP-1 or anywhere else in Sarajevo would have been heard, whether it was from Muslim territory or from direct related Bosnian Army territory. That's what we stated. And there was no sound of outgoing rounds anywhere in that area, only the sound and the vision of incoming round, so the explosions, itself, in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time to call up the UN document which states -- that is P1145, which said that there were 108 explosions during the reporting period. This is the 28th of August, until 5.00 p.m. that day. But, please, can you explain to us: How is it possible that your observers heard one explosion, while there were actually two explosions?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I don't know. There -- I only can say what my observers heard or saw, which is in the statements. I do not recall that there was an idea about two explosions. So if they said they heard one explosion, the two on the OP-1, I assume that you mean those two, that if they have stated that they heard one explosion and saw one explosion, because they saw it as well, then that's their statement, and that fits with the fact that there was one explosion at the Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 200 metres from Markale, before this fifth shell, four more shells dropped. Those four shells, no one -- none of your people heard them. Secondly, even though four shells dropped at a distance of 400 metres away, Markale was full of people who were waiting for the fifth shell. How can you explain these illogical things? How come your observers did not record four incoming shells, the explosions that could be heard, and how do you explain that nobody sought shelter after four 120-millimetre shells fell?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The last point, I cannot explain, because I don't know what people thought and what people heard on the moment that the Markale projectile exploded and the four projectiles exploded before.
