And as far as I can recall, my people at the OP-1 recorded those four projectiles, indeed, and they can be found back in the report of the UNMO HQ of Sarajevo to the UNMO HQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, with all due respect, your associate, Mr. Knustadt, stated that he heard the explosion of an explosive device. If I may call up 1D2826 now, 1D2826 in the e-court, "Explosive Devices." Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, is it usual for a military expert to use the term "explosive device" instead of saying "mortar shells"?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I would like first to read what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3, please, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is in the language I cannot read, and so I have no comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I will read you, and if I can ask --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we not have it in the English version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a technical misstep by the Defence. Can we ask, then, to put up the English original. If I can read the paragraph until we get the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, put your question. You already asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can print up the statement, if need be. It's -- yeah. It's going to take a few minutes to print up the statement, but I think that's better, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we don't have it in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how could you print it? It's on a separate hard-drive. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting: In paragraph 72 of your consolidated statement, it says: [In English] "I talked with two UNMOs on my team, Major Conway and Major Knustadt, who manned OP-1. They reported to me that they did not observe any outgoing shots from the Bosnian-held territory." [Interpretation] Do you know that they also said that nothing flew over them either?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That might have been that they have said that or I would read that. And, again, I cannot not judge their -- I cannot deny their explanations or their testimonies, but I would really like to read that so that I can judge it myself, what they exactly said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was too enthusiastic. There's two diagrams that were attached to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the one about whom you corrected the spelling, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Page 3, please: "OP, as previously stated --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "OP, as previously stated ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Sorry? I don't understand what was said. I don't -- it was quite soft. What is the question, because I'm puzzled, what I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. He asked to read that part first, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which part do I have to read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The third paragraph, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's some sort of confusion with this translation. I'm not sure where this is going. Can we -- leave this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, on the scene, itself, were you under pressure by the investigating team to pronounce yourself as soon as possible on the direction of fire? Just leave it while we organise ourselves. Well, let me try to assist you. It's P150, page 2, the manuscript, where the B/C/S translation says: "The investigating team invested great efforts to prove that the attack originated from the Serb side. That was probably because of the unusual use of heavy mortars, but there is no hard evidence for that." And then you say in another place that: "The Bosnian part of the team asked you to determine, as quickly as possible, that the shell was a Serbian one." It's page 2 of this document. Pardon. [In English] "The investigation" -- [Interpretation] Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that seems to be the last paragraph on this page. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Collapse this B/C/S version. Did you read that passage, Mr. Konings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it can be made a bit larger, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wonder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear to me, yeah. But I still don't know what the question is, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is: Was the investigating team making efforts to prove that this projectile came from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The investigation team was making a lot of efforts in order to try to find the origin of fire. And being a Bosnian Army investigation team, it seemed logical that they tried to prove that it came from the Serb side. Besides, I understand that a war was going on there. But you can read in paragraph number 3 what my conclusion was at the end of the day of 28 of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's written here, Lieutenant-Colonel, is that efforts were made to prove that Serbs were to blame, not the origin of fire. And then it says since a heavy mortar is involved -- are you going to tell me that the Muslim side had no heavy mortars in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not telling you anything, and I do not state that. I do not understand the question. It's suddenly a jump from one issue to another issue, which I do not understand what you -- what you're really asking me now. I'm not -- I never stated or never said anything that the Muslims did not have heavy mortars inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it says that this is impossible, due to the use of heavy mortars, so it's -- there's no evidence to blame it on the Serbs, so what is the reason? Why was this blamed on the Serbs? I'm just stating that Muslims also had heavy mortars in the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: The patrol report that is now in front of me has seen -- has a piece of information, as I explained before, which is counted together by the UN organisation, by UNPROFOR, to make a complete picture of what happened on the 28 of August. This patrol report is written at the end of -- on the 28th. On that moment in time, and only on that moment in time, I came to these patrol leader's remarks. On that moment in time, I had nothing further to add to what I saw and to what my -- I even didn't make any conclusions, because conclusions had to be made by my high-ranking superiors. It's something that they did later on. During the later days, the commander of UNPROFOR came to the conclusion that the round came from the Serb side. I never made that conclusion. On the moment in time that this report was written, the remark, as stated there, the investigation team tried very hard to prove that the attack came from the Serb side, and the investigation team is the overall investigation team of which we were a kind of observation part. Due to the normal use of heavy mortars, that is likely, that's my own conclusion, but there is no hard proof on this fact. That was stated on the moment in time on the 28 of August, which is, I think, very clear. It doesn't say anything about the fact whether the Muslim Army had 120s, yes or no. There is no -- no relevance to that in this moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By excluding the possibility that the shell came from the separation line or the positions of the BH Army, you drew two conclusions; first of all, that the observers at OP-1 did not hear outgoing fire, and, two, that it was not militarily justified to use the first charge on a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand the question. I only can say that we observed -- what we observed is that there was a round at Markale. My observers did not hear or see any outgoing rounds from their vicinity, from the Bosnian Army territory, or even from the confrontation line where also Bosnian Serbs were. That's one thing. The second thing is the term "militarily justifies to use the first charge," I never used that. I only have said that in our view, the view of the Royal Netherlands Army, we hardly -- we seldom or never use the lowest charge of a mortar. That's a military habit that we use, because when you use a 120 with a lower charge, propelling charge, I mean, then it will explode in the vicinity of your own troops, which is quite dangerous. So we don't use that. But it is of non-interest here, because there were no outgoing rounds from the vicinity of OP-1, so the charge that has been used must have been bigger than charge O, charge 1, or even charge 2. And that's not only my conclusion. That's also the conclusion of the commander of UNPROFOR which came out a few days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I wanted to let you know that you will have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that this witness has not ben examined. Regardless of my amateurism, he has not been examined, not even on the subject of Markale, let alone anything else. Just for Markale, I need one more hour. I must ask the Trial Chamber to give me another 90 minutes, one session, tomorrow for this witness, for Markale specifically. Certain statements have been made that we have to refute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I made it clear on several occasions that we'll stick to the time-limit this time. You didn't hear me at all. If you couldn't cover all the points you wanted to cover, so be it. I take it you don't have many items to cover during your re-examination, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it would be impractical to call another witness until the end of the day, then, you'll have about 15 minutes to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, is it true that the angle of descent of this shell could have been 67 degrees or more, but certainly not less?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's our conclusion, 76 [sic] degrees or more, yes. It is wrong on the text. It's 60 -- it now says "67." It now says "76," it should be "67."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, 67. Can we now ask for 1D2830. 1830 -- sorry, 2830. Please look, Lieutenant-Colonel, at this diagram. If we take it that this angle on either side was 67 degrees, would you, with your knowledge of firing tables, say that these distances correspond to the charges? Would, for instance, the first charge, 0 plus 1, reach to about 900 metres; 0 plus 2 would have a range of 1600; 0 plus 3 would have a range of 2500, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what this diagram is explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then agree, Lieutenant-Colonel, that the apex of these trajectories would also have to be as drawn here? The lowest charge would be over 500 metres in height, the next one 900 metres, the third one 1400 metres, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I guess that this diagram is correct. So if you read the diagram, it states the culmination point of every projectile fired with a specific round, under theoretical conditions, which I think that this is, coming from a firing table, and it states how -- or what the culmination point, as we call it, from a round is using a certain -- certain propelling charge, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go any further with this document, which is headed in a language I don't understand, can we found out, actually, what it purports to represent?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain. This is a graphic chart, Judge, of firing tables with different charges with an angle of descent of 67 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did you get this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a manual with firing tables. We can show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it an excerpt from a book or is it something that was produced by the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a manual, a firing manual including firing tables, and on this table, on this chart, we see trajectories with various charges. The only constant here is the angle of descent. It has to be 67 degrees or more. Otherwise, the projectile would have gone through the building. So the lowest possible angle of descent is 67 degrees. These are measurements that apply to various charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was asking about the source of this document, but you didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firing tables for 120-millimetre mortars. It's a manual, a military book, published in 1982. It's a manual for our mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is this diagram produced by the Defence team on the basis of that manual? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, those are firing elements for various charges. Anyone can check. Anyone can check in the book, and the lieutenant-colonel has already recognised this diagram as a visualisation of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies. I kept you waiting. Ms. Edgerton, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No apology required, Your Honour. I would be prepared to accept the actual firing table for the mortar produced -- for that batch of mortars produced at the period of time that the artefact which caused the deaths at Markale II was manufactured from that particular factory. I understand these firing tables are specific to batches of weapons, batches produced at particular factories at particular times, and I have no assurance, based on what we've heard so far, that this represents that, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see how it goes. But the topic you raised, maybe it's a proper topic for your redirect, possibly. We'll hear the remainder of your cross-examination. What is your question in relation to this diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will present the tables as well. We have an up-loaded document with tables. Can we now see 1D2231; the same thing, only with a radar drawn in. Until then, before we see 1D2231, I would like to say to Ms. Edgerton that these are tables for all charges. It is a standard thing does not vary from case to case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, do you recall that the Cymbeline radar was operating, and the lower -- lowest limit at which it would register a projectile was set to 548 metres? So if the charge was 0 plus 1, and if it had been fired 900 metres into Muslim territory, it would have been registered. That's what we see, that the setting was to 548 metres, and even the apex of the first shell for the first charge would have been recorded. May I ask you once again. You claim, or at least it's your position, that this shell that came from the Serb territory from a distance of more than 2500 metres somehow slipped below the radar beam of the Cymbelin radar which was set to 548 metres on the lower end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I actually have a lot of trouble with this question because the question is being asked based on a document that assumes the -- excuse me -- that assumes the center point of the Cymbelin radar, and we have no information to be able to determine whether or not that assertion is accurate. We don't know where the center point of the radar might have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I add to that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about it. I am not aware about the capabilities of the Cymbelin radar. I don't know which settings it had that day. It was an UNPROFOR radar. It was not controlled by the UNMOs. I had no with them before or after the incident. I know that in the G-2 UNPROFOR report, there is something mentioned about the Cymbelin radar, but I cannot add any information to that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, let us look at 09917. That's 65 ter 09917.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "Every projectile fired in such a way that its trajectory runs below the radar beam had to come from a place at a distance of between 1.050 and 3.500 metres." You claim that this shell came from the Serbian side. Can we see page 3 now. So you are aware of the radar, you know at which height the radar was able to register shells, and you claim that this shell had to be fired from a distance greater than 1.050 metres in order to slip below the radar beam. Look at this paragraph 4. That's your report, where you say that the radar was set --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, that's not his report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a UN report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not my report. It's a report from HQ UNPROFOR, which I had nothing to do with. I only provided the proper information which we discussed before. Cymbelin radar was not under my command. I had nothing to do with that, so the statement which is on the screen now is "HQ UNPROFOR." I think that was stated on the first page. It's not my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are an artillery man, Lieutenant-Colonel. Are you trying to say that this mortar shell, coming from a greater distance, would have a lower trajectory?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I'm not stating anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But based on your experience and based on these tables and the diagram I showed you, would it be possible for this mortar shell to fly horizontally, if fired from a greater distance, and to slip below the radar beam or not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I do think I'm not in a position to comment upon those two diagrams that I only was briefly possible to look upon, so I refrain from having any comments on the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Regardless of any diagrams, Lieutenant-Colonel, first of all, would it help you if you could look at the tables, and, tell us, is it possible to avoid the radar firing from Serb territory? Was it possible to fire this weapon in such a way that the shell would fly below 548 metres in height?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your question, that regardless of the radar, whether a projectile could fly below 548 metres? Can you answer the question, if that is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all respect, Your Honour, I -- I don't understand the question. The point is that a mortar projectile -- I'm an experienced artillery and mortar man. A mortar projectile has a high angle, is a high-angle projectile, which means that it flies on high angles, on high -- a certain height. Each angle that you fire it with has a separate angle of impact, so you really need a firing table in order to find out where we are talking about. I'm not willing to discuss anything anymore until I have proper tables in front of me and the capability to study that. And I already said before that I do not know the specifics of the Cymbelin radar. I know the specifics of the radar in my own army, but I do not know the specifics of the Cymbelin radar, not at that time, it was not required to me, not at this time, so I cannot say -- I cannot add anything valuable to this question or to these remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph 4, it says that it is assessed that if this projectile wanted to avoid the radar, it would have to be fired from a greater distance to achieve a lower trajectory. Now, you, as an artilleryman, just confirmed that a mortar cannot be fired directly; that is to say, from a greater distance, the trajectory would be higher, not lower; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That's not what I said. Everything is taken out of proportion. There is a trajectory that belongs to each charge and each angle of fire that you used. And the generic basics of a mortar projectile is that it is a high-angle projectile, but on each distance that you use, each charge that you use, it has a different height, a different culmination point. So that's the only thing I can say. And, again, in combination with the radar beam, as is suggested here, I cannot say anything about it. I don't know how much time -- how often I have to repeat that. I don't know the specifics of the Cymbelin radar on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the time is up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The time is up, but I will allow you to ask one last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the Trial Chamber to ask the witness to create a chart on the basis of tables that we will provide to him, how this shell could have come in at an angle of 67 degrees and had evaded the beam of the radar? This shell could not have come in like that. The radar missed it, nobody saw it, but the radar had to have registered it, because it's not possible for it to happen any other way. I mean, it's difficult, with a witness who does not wish to co-operate, to complete our cross-examination, and these proceedings are coming to the point where there is a danger of its regularity being disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be analysed by the future lawyers and historians later on. Do you have any redirect examination, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, you heard earlier, at page 104, lines 7 and 8, that firing tables are a standard thing does not vary from case to case. Now, you've said just a few moments ago you're a mortar man. Is that your experience of firing tables?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: A firing table is a thing that is, indeed, for a generic -- a generic thing. It's a theoretical basis of every artillery or mortar weapon. It's not a -- indeed, not a basis -- situation-to-situation related. It is a generic book wherein you find all the theoretical data of a weapons system in combination with ammunition, and that book is prepared or is produced on the moment that the mortar is produced and that a lot of test firing is done. From there, you -- from there, in the practical situation, you do measurements of weather, of wind direction, wind speed, temperature of the propelling charges, in order to make everything more correct. So in the basis, the firing table is not a case-to-case scenario, it's a generic book that can be used for 120, in general, or 155, or whatever weapons system you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So then given what you've just said, that the book is prepared or produced at the moment that the mortar is produced, and that a lot of test firing is done, let me ask you the following: Is there the likelihood of some variation in results, depending on the individual mortar batches, and the test results as well?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: As I said, the book is a generic book. The book is based on -- as far as I know, from my own experience in the NATO army, is based upon firing a lot of rounds and making -- and making calculations, and bringing that all together in the book. What you need to do is -- batches of ammunition that are produced can have different data, they differ from each other, so they are -- they are produced under controlled situations, but they, nevertheless, differ. There is even a difference between each weapons system. Each weapons system has a different muzzle velocity, each weapons system -- although you use the same batch of ammunition. That's a variety that is -- well, that is related to military arms, to arms in general. So you can use the theoretical data that are in the firing table, but in practice you need extra data according to the weather, the ammunition, the specific batch of ammunition that you have used. You gather that, you collect that, and you use that. That's the practice that we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did not use my last question. You promised me a last question, but then you gave the floor to Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask to have P1959 in the e-court. That was admitted today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, sir, what would you say if I were to tell you that based on the incoming line that you stated, the line of separation was not 1.050 metres but was greater than 2.000 metres? Would you agree that Colina Kapa was in Muslim hands? Do you see this? This is south of OP-1. There is Pogladine [phoen] and then Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have no detailed recollection of where exactly the confrontation line was running in that moment, so I have nothing to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree you can see here on the scale that one little square is actually one kilometre? 94 and 95 are exactly 1 kilometre apart, and there is a scale between them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: 94 and 95, the squares are 1 by 1, but -- that's true, but I don't understand the question, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is : You can see the scale. Is that the measure of one kilometre, and then can you tell how far Colina Kapa is from number 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Konings has already answered that question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In his reports and in their reports, it figures that it's 1.050 metres, where the Muslim territory or the line is, and that is the criteria on the basis of which it was determined that it was the Serbs who fired. But I'm saying that this distance is closer to 3.000 than to 1.050 metres. And we know Colina Kapa was in Muslim hands the whole time. We see 5. We know where the line of separation was. So the distance is 3 kilometres, and so this is one of the irregularities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, could you give the reference where he said -- he answered the question as to the distance from -- distance between number 5 and Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The answer was actually at page 111, lines 8 to 10, where he said he had no detailed recollection of exactly where the confrontation line was running in that moment, so he had nothing to say on that. And the question finished with: "This is south of OP-1. There is Pogladine and then Colina Kapa." Immediately before that: "Would you agree that Colina Kapa was in Muslim hands?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Having had the benefit of looking at the map again, I wonder whether you can answer the question as to the distance between number 5 and Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to measure it carefully. But if I looked to that, I would assume that it is about between 2.000 and 2.500 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Konings, and I thank you very much for your coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll rise for today, and we'll resume tomorrow at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of December, 2010, at 11.15 a.m.
